papers.abstract: Within the minimally extended Standard Model (MESM), with Dirac neutrinos, we study fermion propagation in the electroweak-symmetric plasma, where the Higgs expectation value vanishes. We show that the zero-temperature mass eigenstates do not coincide with the left-handed fermionic quasiparticles identified by the thermal medium, while the right-handed fermions remain diagonal in this basis. At the leading hard-thermal-loop (HTL) order, the left-handed fermion self-energies form flavor matrices containing the CKM and PMNS mixing structures. Diagonalizing flavor matrices, we show that the two members of each left-handed weak doublet possess identical leading-HTL thermal spectra. The eigenvalues are CP-even and are invariant under weak-basis transformations. In this symmetric-phase thermal basis, the leading HTL fermion propagators and electroweak gauge interactions are diagonal, while the flavor structure is transferred to the Yukawa interactions. We further express the HTL effective Lagrangian in this basis, derive the corresponding dispersion relations, and numerically compare the eigenvalues of the complete leading-HTL matrices with the diagonal thermal coefficients obtained in the broken-phase mass basis. This construction provides a diagonal HTL description of fermionic quasiparticles and a systematic framework for resummation and higher-order corrections in the electroweak-symmetric plasma.

papers.title: Structural Origins of Cubic Complexity in Pebble Motion
papers.abstract: The pebble motion problem (PMP) asks whether labeled pebbles on a graph can be rearranged by moving them to adjacent empty vertices (blanks). Kornhauser, Miller, and Spirakis (FOCS 1984) proved the tight $Θ(N^3)$ worst-case bound on $N$-vertex graphs and asked for efficient approximation of move counts. Whether this bound is tight on trees remained open for over four decades. We give the first $\mathrm{o}(N^3)$ upper bound on trees: every feasible instance admits an $\mathrm{O}(N^2\log N)$-move solution, constructible in time linear in its length, within a logarithmic factor of the known $Ω(N^2)$ lower bound. We extend the tree method to a hybrid algorithm with structure-dependent bounds for general graphs. When $2\leq N-n=\mathrm{O}(1)$, every instance on a feasible puzzle admits an $\mathrm{O}(n\,\mathrm{CL}(G)\,\mathrm{D}(G))$-move solution, where $n$ counts pebbles, $\mathrm{D}(G)$ is the diameter, and $\mathrm{CL}(G)$ is the maximum shortest-cycle length through a vertex. For square grids, this matches the classical $\mathrm{O}(N^{3/2})$ bound. Cubic complexity requires $\mathrm{O}(1)$ blanks. We develop cut-vertex reconfiguration and a closure theorem under arbitrary ear extensions. These imply that cubic complexity requires a unique biconnected component $X$ of order $Θ(N)$ with reconfiguration cost $Θ(N^3)$; the total attachment through each cut vertex of $G$ in $X$ has bounded order. Moreover, $X$ has no cycle of unbounded sublinear order, and intersecting $Θ(N)$-cycles in $X$ share at least $N-n$ vertices. Attaching bounded-size connected graphs along $\mathrm{O}(1)$ individual edges of a $Θ(N)$-cycle yields cubic complexity for feasible puzzles, whereas two $Θ(N)$-cycles sharing one vertex have worst-case complexity $Θ(N^2\log N)$. We conjecture that this construction characterizes the cubic regime.

papers.title: Collision Risk Estimation via Loss Prediction in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Collision risk estimation and avoidance play central roles in the safety of autonomous driving (AD) systems. Recently emerged end-to-end AD systems gain collision avoidance ability by minimizing losses to penalize planning trajectories that are too close to other objects. Despite a significant collision rate during testing, most end-to-end planners do not explicitly quantify the collision risk in their outputs. To address this, we introduce RiskMonitor, an efficient plug-and-play module that interprets planning and motion tokens from state-of-the-art end-to-end planners to estimate collision risk. Inspired by loss prediction based uncertainty quantification, RiskMonitor predicts whether the collision loss -- commonly adopted to train end-to-end planners -- is positive along planned waypoints, framing collision risk estimation as a binary classification task. We evaluate RiskMonitor on the real-world nuScenes dataset (open-loop) and the neural-rendering based simulator, NeuroNCAP (closed-loop). Our token-driven method outperforms prediction-driven approaches, including deterministic rules, Gaussian mixture models, and Monte Carlo Dropout. When integrated with a simple braking policy, RiskMonitor improves collision avoidance ability by $66.5\%$ in a closed-loop test on safety-critical scenarios. These results demonstrate that monitoring collision risk using plan and motion tokens enhances the safety of end-to-end AD without retraining it.

papers.title: On the Efficiency of Structured Pruning in Small Language Model Pretraining
papers.abstract: Companies that deploy generative language models on edge devices often need to train small models from scratch due to legal, data-governance, or product-customization requirements. An alternative approach is to train an enlarged model and compress it to the target size via structured pruning, but this advantage becomes unclear once the cost of pretraining the enlarged model is included. We introduce the enlarge-and-prune framework to study this question under full-cost accounting, and show that conventional enlarge-and-prune pipelines -- which train the enlarged model, prune it, and recover in separate stages -- do not consistently outperform direct small-model training under the same total token budget. To overcome this limitation, we propose IDEA Prune, an integrated enlarge-and-prune pipeline that unifies enlarged model pretraining, iterative structured pruning, and recovery under a single cosine annealing learning rate schedule. In controlled experiments compressing 2.8B models to 1.3B with up to 2T tokens on the same dataset, IDEA Prune consistently outperforms conventional pipelines and modestly improves overall performance relative to the scratch baseline, improving MMLU accuracy to 46.4%, compared with 31.4-33.4% for conventional pipelines. These advantages are preserved after downstream supervised fine-tuning, where IDEA Prune matches or outperforms all baselines of the same size on instruction following, math reasoning, and code generation. Our analysis further reveals that intermediate checkpoints provide more favorable pruning starting points than fully converged ones, and that an enlargement factor of approximately 2.6x yields the best pruned models in the tested regime.

papers.title: Seifert forms and slice Euler characteristic of links
papers.abstract: We define the Witt coindex $β$ of a rational bilinear form (not necessarily symmetric) as the codimension minus dimension of a maximal totally isotropic subspace. Levine gave a computable necessary and sufficient condition for $β=0$, but no algorithm of computation of $β$ had been known when $β>0$. Our main result is a computable necessary and sufficient condition for $β=1$ in the case when the symmetrized form is non-degenerate. As shown by Taylor, all upper bounds of the slice genera of knots based on their Seifert form can be derived from the Witt coindex of the Seifert form. The case of an odd $β$ does not apply to knots but we show that it provides an estimate of the slice Euler characteristic for the links with an even number of components. We illustrate our results with examples where the Witt coindex is used to show that a two-component link does not bound a locally flat cylinder in the four-ball, whereas any other known restriction does not show it.

papers.title: On the Effect of Bounded Rationality in Mixed Duopoly Markets
papers.abstract: Nash equilibrium is a common solution concept that captures strategic interaction in market analysis. However, it assumes that all market participants are fully rational and can compute mutually consistent best responses. Level-k reasoning relaxes this assumption by modeling bounded rationality through finite reasoning depth. In this paper, we consider a variation of Cournot competition that includes two suppliers, both following level-k reasoning. One is a self-interested firm and the other serves as a benevolent social planner. First, we show that social welfare is maximized when the planner is one level more rational than its opponent. Welfare is weakly decreasing as the planner's level moves away from this optimum. We then show that welfare under bounded rationality can differ substantially from welfare at Nash equilibrium. We characterize optimal, expectation-maximizing, and robust maximin strategies for the planner under different amounts of information about its opponent's rationality level. Finally, we show how utility design can improve social welfare by allowing the planner to cooperate with or fight the self-interested firm. Numerical experiments further demonstrate and validate our findings.

papers.title: Extended Set-based Tasks for Multi-task Execution and Prioritization
papers.abstract: The ability of executing multiple tasks simultaneously is an important feature of redundant robotic systems. As a matter of fact, complex behaviors can often be obtained as a result of the execution of several tasks. Moreover, in safety-critical applications, tasks designed to ensure the safety of the robot and its surroundings have to be executed along with other nominal tasks. In such cases, it is also important to prioritize the former over the latter. In this paper, we formalize the definition of extended set-based tasks, i.e., tasks which can be executed by rendering subsets of the task space asymptotically stable or forward invariant using control barrier functions. We propose a formal mathematical representation of such tasks that allows for the execution of more complex and time-varying prioritized stacks of tasks using kinematic and dynamic robot models alike. We present an optimization-based framework which is computationally efficient, accounts for input bounds, and allows for the stable execution of time-varying prioritized stacks of extended set-based tasks. The proposed framework is validated using extensive simulations, quantitative comparisons to the state-of-the-art hierarchical quadratic programming, and experiments with robotic manipulators.

papers.title: Randomized Forward Mode of Automatic Differentiation For Optimization Algorithms
papers.abstract: Reverse mode automatic differentiation (AD) computes a gradient in a single sweep, but at a memory cost that grows with the length of the computational graph. That cost becomes the binding constraint when the graph is long, as in parameter identification governed by differential equations or in training on memory-limited hardware. We study a randomized forward mode gradient (RFG) as an alternative to backpropagation in precisely this regime. RFG is a random gradient estimator built from the directional derivative along a random vector, a quantity that forward mode AD computes without storing a tape. Replacing the gradient with RFG yields a class of optimization algorithms; for RFG-based gradient descent (GD) and Polyak's heavy ball (PHB) methods, we establish convergence results on quadratic functions. The analysis reveals that using random vectors from a probability distribution with the smallest kurtosis yields the fastest rate of convergence. Computational experiments demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithms and verify the theoretical findings, including beyond quadratic functions. We further characterize when RFG is computationally preferable to backpropagation. Since the variance of RFG grows with the parameter dimension $d$ while the memory required by the reverse mode grows with the length $\ell$ of the computational graph, the relevant figure of merit is the ratio $\ell/d$. We confirm this by measurement against reverse mode with checkpointing. For a physics-informed neural network, where $d$ is large and $\ell$ short, RFG is not competitive. For parameter identification governed by differential equations, where a handful of coefficients is recovered from a long time integration, RFG requires one to three orders of magnitude less memory. The price is a larger iteration count, which leaves its time to solution comparable to or worse than a well-tuned reverse mode.

papers.title: Geometric Manin's Conjecture for Fano 3-Folds
papers.abstract: We classify families of free rational curves on all smooth Fano threefolds over the complex numbers. In particular, we prove the family of very free rational curves representing any fixed numerical curve class is either irreducible or empty. This proves Geometric Manin's Conjecture in dimension three. For general Fano threefolds of each deformation type, our results allow us to explicitly count the number of components of the moduli space of irreducible, geometrically rational curves, which may not be free, representing any numerical class.

papers.title: The homotopy types of $Sp(n)$-gauge groups over $S^{4m}$
papers.abstract: Let $m$ and $n$ be two positive integers such that $m < n$, and let $Q_{n-m+1}$ be the symplectic quasi-projective space of rank $n-m+1$. Denote by $P_{n,k}$ the principal $\mathrm{Sp(n)}$-bundle over $S^{4m}$ and $\mathcal{G}_{k,m}(\mathrm{Sp(n)})$ be the gauge group of $P_{n,k}$ classified by $k\varepsilon'$, where $\varepsilon'$ is a generator of $π_{4m}(B(\mathrm{Sp(n)}))\cong\mathbb{Z}$. In this article, first, we will study the order of the Samelson product $S^{4m-1}\wedge Q_{n-m+1}\rightarrow \mathrm{Sp(n)}$. Then, by the unstable $K$-theory method, we will partially classify the homotopy types of $\mathcal{G}_{k,m}(\mathrm{Sp(n)})$ by giving a lower bound for the number of homotopy types of $\mathcal{G}_{k,m}(\mathrm{Sp(n)})$.

papers.title: Vanishing results for the coherent cohomology of automorphic vector bundles over the Siegel variety in positive characteristic
papers.abstract: We prove vanishing results for the coherent cohomology of the good reduction modulo $p$ of the Siegel variety with coefficients in some automorphic bundles. We show that for an automorphic bundle with highest weight $λ$ near the walls of the anti-dominant Weyl chamber, there is an integer $e \geq 0$ such that the cohomology is concentrated in degrees $[0, e]$. The accessible weights with our method are not necessarily regular and not necessarily $p$-small. Since our method is technical, we also provide an algorithm written in Sage that computes explicitly the vanishing results.

papers.title: Visualizing the geometry of labeled high-dimensional data with spheres
papers.abstract: Data visualizations can summarize high-dimensional distributions in two or three dimensions. Dimensionality reduction entails a loss of information, and what is preserved differs between methods. Existing methods preserve the local or the global geometry of the points, and most techniques do not consider labels. Here we introduce "hypersphere2sphere" (H2S), a new method that aims to visualize not the points, but the relationships between the labeled distributions. H2S fits a hypersphere to each labeled set of points in the high-dimensional space of the original data and visualizes each hypersphere as a sphere in 3D (or a circle in 2D). H2S perfectly captures the geometry of up to 4 high-dimensional hyperspheres using spheres in 3D (or 3 using circles in 2D), and approximates the geometry for larger numbers of distributions, matching the sizes (radii), and the pairwise separations (between-center distances) and the overlaps (along the center-connection line). The resulting visualizations are robust to sampling imbalances. Leveraging labels and the sphere as the simplest geometrical primitive, H2S provides an important addition to the toolbox of visualization techniques.

papers.title: Hilbert's Tenth problem and NP-completeness of Boolean Syllogistic with unordered cartesian product
papers.abstract: We relate the decidability problem for BS with unordered cartesian product with Hilbert's Tenth problem and prove that BS with unordered cartesian product is NP-complete.

papers.title: On $β=6$ Tracy-Widom distribution and the second Calogero-Painlevé system
papers.abstract: The Calogero-Painlevé systems were introduced in 2001 by K. Takasaki as a natural generalization of the classical Painlevé equations to the case of the several Painlevé ``particles'' coupled via the Calogero type interactions. In 2014, I. Rumanov discovered the remarkable fact that a particular case of the second Calogero-Painlevé II equation describes the Tracy-Widom distribution function for the general beta-ensembles with even values of the parameter beta. Most recently, in 2017 work of M. Bertola, M. Cafasso, and V. Rubtsov, it was proven that all Calogero-Painlevé systems are Lax integrable, and hence their solutions admit a Riemann-Hilbert representation. This important observation has opened the door to rigorous, based on the Deift-Zhou nonlinear steepest descent method, asymptotic analysis of the Calogero-Painlevé equations. This in turn yields the possibility of rigorous evaluation of the asymptotic behavior of the Tracy-Widom distributions for the values of beta beyond the classical $β=1, 2, 4.$ In this work we shall start an asymptotic analysis of the Calogero-Painlevé system with a special focus on the Calogero-Painlevé system corresponding to $β= 6$ Tracy-Widom distribution function. The principle technical challenge is the implementation of the nonlinear steepest descent approach beyond the $2\times 2$ matrix dimension of the corresponding Riemann-Hilbert problem; in our case, it is $6\times 6$.

papers.title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.

papers.title: Spin-adapted state preparation for quantum chemistry
papers.abstract: Quantum phase estimation for strongly-correlated molecules requires an initial state of high overlap with the true ground state, and preparing one is a significant fault-tolerant cost. Matrix product states (MPS) produced by the density matrix renormalisation group (DMRG) are a leading choice, yet existing circuits treat their tensors as dense or do not use the full symmetries present in molecular electronic Hamiltonians. In quantum chemistry, DMRG also exploits total spin, a non-abelian symmetry, storing one amplitude per spin multiplet instead of one per state. We show that the reduced tensors of such a spin-adapted MPS, labelled by the steps of the unitary group approach, form an abelian-symmetric MPS, which existing block-sparse preparation protocols can load at a cost set by the multiplet count. One state-independent rotation per site, determined by a Clebsch-Gordan coefficient, then returns the state to the occupation basis. We provide resource estimates for our circuits on singlet ground states of active space models of iron-sulphur clusters, finding improvements in Toffoli count up to $135\times$ compared to dense methods and $4.9\times$ compared to block-sparse methods applied to the same states, with up to $3.7\times$ fewer ancilla qubits required.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
papers.abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

papers.title: RTLDetective: Agentic RTL Debugging through Dataflow Analysis and Simulation-Guided Fault Localization
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promise in RTL debugging, yet accurately localizing functional errors and generating reliable repairs remain challenging. We propose RTLDetective, a multi-agent framework that integrates signal dependency analysis, simulation-guided fault localization, and knowledge-based reasoning for automated RTL debugging and repair. RTLDetective constructs signal dependency graphs from RTL code and extracts failure information from waveform traces. A lightweight localizer agent predicts expected intermediate signal values and evaluates them through targeted simulation interventions, iteratively probing signal dependencies to isolate suspicious logic and identify potential fault locations. A debug agent combines this evidence with static analysis, a curated knowledge base of hardware design principles and RTL bug patterns, and reasoning to generate corrected RTL. To reduce inference overhead, the framework reuses cached context across debugging iterations. We evaluate RTLDetective on the MEIC benchmark, achieving an 86.1% fix rate, 13.9 percentage points above the best baseline, while making fewer LLM calls.

papers.title: PRETZEL: A Benchmark for Cyclic Peptide Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: Macrocyclic peptides are a growing therapeutic modality, and co-folding models are increasingly used to predict their structures. Yet published evaluations rely on small, loosely curated target sets that differ from paper to paper, so results are not comparable, and most report pose RMSD alone, without checking whether the predicted molecule is chemically correct. We introduce PRETZEL (Prediction of Ring-Enclosed Topology: Zero-shot Evaluation of cycLic peptides), a benchmark of 285 curated cyclic peptide-protein complexes spanning three cyclization chemistries, all post-dating the training cutoff of every model evaluated. PRETZEL has three components: PRETZEL-SET, an evaluation set annotated by cyclization chemistry and chemical novelty; PRETZEL-TWIST, a specification layer that compiles a single canonical macrocycle description into each engine's native input format and verifies the returned structure; and PRETZEL-SALT, an evaluation suite pairing standard pose metrics with validity checks for bond distances, bond angles, dihedrals, and ring closure. Using these, we evaluate AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, Protenix-v2, and HighFold3. Protenix-v2 achieves the best median RMSD at 9.05 A, with 19.3% of predictions under 2 A and 37.5% under 5 A. Accuracy varies by cyclization chemistry: models handle head-to-tail macrocycles relatively well but degrade on stapled targets. Chemical validity is weaker still: at most 8.1% of predictions have a fully valid set of inter-residue bonds, and no engine closes every macrocycle in more than 80.7% of its predictions, so pose accuracy alone is an insufficient criterion. These failures share a cause: co-folding models place macrocycles without representing them, treating cyclization and non-canonical chemistry as annotations layered onto a residue sequence rather than as first-class structure. PRETZEL is released with all inputs, predictions, and evaluation code.

papers.title: An entropy-adjusted invariant likelihood for incidental parameters
papers.abstract: Incidental parameters can make maximum likelihood inconsistent in short panels. When they act through a known translation group, integration with respect to Haar measure eliminates them exactly and gives an invariant likelihood, whose score is shown to be the conditional expectation, given the maximal invariant, of the Neyman-orthogonalised score of every order. Under interactive fixed effects the orbit is an unknown factor space, and the invariant score for it has a drift equal to minus the derivative of the entropy of the retained contrasts. An entropy adjustment removes this drift and, at the true structural parameter, identifies the factor space uniquely when the loadings span it. The adjusted estimating equations are the gradient of a single criterion if and only if the entropy separates into an orbit term and an error-law term, as in scale and elliptical families; consistency then follows from a design condition, and in general from an equilibrium-identification condition, with asymptotic normality for fixed panel length. A boundary is derived for recovering a skewness sign discarded by a two-period invariant reduction. An application to Vietnamese rice farming rejects equal household-effect weights across survey waves and finds lower returns to scale.

papers.title: Stopping criteria in structural reliability analysis: An overview
papers.abstract: Stopping criteria have become a crucial component of probabilistic and statistical methods in structural reliability analysis, helping prevent structural defects and failures, as well as inaccurate evaluations of existing structures. Over time, these rules have evolved in both concept and application, whereas their treatment in the literature remains fragmented. They are often developed and presented in connection with specific models or analytical frameworks, obscuring their broader applicability across diverse models and methodologies. On this basis, the aim of this article is twofold. First, it overviews a wide range of stopping rules, drawing on concepts from applied probability and statistics. These strategies include classical methods based on error estimates or variance, and stability detection. While many of these ideas were developed in other fields, they have the potential to offer useful tools for structural reliability tasks like managing sampling, improving surrogate models, and checking for convergence. Second, this article introduces a structured framework to organize past and recent developments in this area. It brings together various stopping criteria, clarifies their conceptual roles, explains their theoretical foundations, and compares their practical strengths and limitations. By relating these methods to common modeling and methodological practices, and by incorporating a systematic comparison of performance aspects such as accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, we aim to identify dominant strategies, highlight shared challenges, and point to directions for further progress.

papers.title: FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation
papers.abstract: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/

papers.title: Multi-vantage SO/PHI and SDO/HMI magnetic field observations of active region NOAA 13465
papers.abstract: Context. Until the launch of Solar Orbiter, long term studies of active region magnetic fields were restricted to a single vantage point: that from Earth. What further restricted these studies were geometrical effects, such as foreshortening and projection, that plague magnetic field observations when the active region was away from the central meridian. Aims. To track an active region, in this case NOAA 13465, with Solar Orbiter during a perihelion pass and use co-observations made by SDO/HMI and SO/PHI-HRT from different vantage points to explore the systematics plaguing observations away from disc centre. Methods. We use the SHARP (Space-Weather HMI Active Region Patches) data series from SDO/HMI, and create similar datasets with SO/PHI-HRT observations. We compare and contrast the line-of-sight and the three heliographic magnetic field components. Finally we compare the unsigned radial flux, and unsigned totals of the northward and westward magnetic components using the SHARP masking method to select a common area. Results. We find that the instrument observing closer to the limb infers a greater unsigned radial magnetic flux compared to that observing at disc centre, with a maximum near approximately $45^\circ$. The plage displayed more susceptibility to resolution and projection effects than the active region's sole sunspot. In particular the deduced area of the solar plage drove the observed increase in flux near the limb. Thanks to its higher spatial resolution, the SO/PHI-HRT data showed a smaller effect compared to SDO/HMI near the limb, highlighting a dependence on instrument resolution. Finally, the ratio of the two instruments' vertical magnetic flux exhibits a strong positive correlation with the ratio of the cosine of the instruments' viewing angles.

papers.title: E-Waste-Bench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Visual Triage of Data-Center Hardware
papers.abstract: Retired data-center hardware can often be refurbished or resold, but triage demands more than object categories. A model must tell visually similar parts apart, judge condition under damage and occlusion, and read the printed part number. We audit nine public e-waste collections. They cover mostly consumer devices (only 10% of images are labeled as a data-center part), label neither condition nor printed text, and contain 42% exact or augmented duplicates. We introduce E-Waste-Bench, 328K photographs drawn from 762K deduplicated images and labeled for class (24 classes), granularity, condition and printed text. Images come from those collections and the web, where a recipe-based crawler works beside an agent built on an open-weight vision-language model. The agent vets new sources and reads sites the crawler cannot parse, and both are steered toward under-represented classes. Training labels are model-made, splits follow near-duplicate groups, and human annotators label a test set of nearly 10,000 images. We benchmark classification, condition, detection, text perception and cross-dataset transfer. On this test set, a ConvNeXt-T trained on E-Waste-Bench reaches 64.3% top-1, against 31.5% with the public collections alone. Near-duplicate leakage inflates top-1 by 3.0 points under model-made test labels but by less than 0.1 under human labels, so model-labeled benchmarks need group splits. Accuracy falls to 42.1% on marketplace and auction photographs, the closest proxy for hardware leaving service. Data and code will be released.

papers.title: A Sharp Lower Bound for the First Nonzero Steklov Eigenvalue of the Witten Laplacian on Weighted Surfaces with Nonnegative Bakry-Emery-Ricci Tensor
papers.abstract: We consider compact connected weighted surfaces with smooth boundary whose Bakry-Emery-Ricci tensor is nonnegative. We assume that the geodesic curvature of the boundary is bounded below in terms of the normal and tangential derivatives of the weight function. Under these assumptions, we prove a lower bound for the first nonzero Steklov eigenvalue of the Witten Laplacian, which is sharp in the sense that equality holds if and only if the surface is isometric to a Euclidean disk and the weight function is constant.

papers.title: Variational Thresholds and Multiplicity for a Nonlocal r-Laplacian Logistic-Type Problem
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the existence, multiplicity and asymptotic behavior of solutions to a class of nonlocal logistic-type problems with the \(r\)-Laplacian operator in the fast diffusion regime: %, with a real parameter $λ$: \[ \begin{cases} -Δ_r u - \displaystyle\int_Ω K(x,y)u(y)\,dy = a(x)u +λ|u|^{q-2}u \displaystyle\int_ΩQ(x,y)|u(y)|^q\,dy, & x\in Ω, \\[0.4em] u = 0, & x\in \partialΩ. \end{cases} \] The model has local diffusion, nonlocal dispersal, and nonlinear global interactions, and depends on a real parameter $λ$. For $λ\ge 0$, we establish the existence of nonnegative weak solutions via a variational principle. In the case \(λ<0\), we characterize two variational thresholds, \(-\infty<\widehatλ^*<λ^*<0\), which separate different solution intervals. For \(λ^*<λ<0\), the energy functional has a global minimizer with negative energy and a mountain-pass critical point with positive energy, yielding two distinct nontrivial weak solutions. The same holds at \(λ=λ^*\), where the global minimizer has zero energy. In a left neighborhood of \(λ^*\), two distinct nontrivial weak solutions persist, a local minimizer and a mountain-pass critical point, both with positive energy and the latter at a strictly higher level. For \(λ<\widehatλ^*\), only the trivial solution exists. Finally, as $λ\to 0^-$, the norm of the global minimizers blows up. Along subsequences, selected nonnegative mountain-pass solutions converge strongly in $W_0^{1,r}(Ω)$ as $λ\to 0$ to a nontrivial nonnegative weak solution of the problem at $λ= 0$. The associated mountain-pass levels converge to the same limit from both sides of zero, and the corresponding solution norms also converge to a common value.

papers.title: Collateral Architecture and Correlated Slashing in Liquid Restaking
papers.abstract: Liquid restaking protocols allow pooled stake to support multiple slashable commitments, creating an allocation problem in which additional rewards must be balanced against correlated slash claims. This risk depends not only on dependence between slash events, but also on how collateral is allocated or reused across commitments. We develop a unified model ranging from unique stake, where capital is divided among positions, to shared collateral, where the same capital supports multiple commitments. We show that portfolio variance is governed jointly by gross exposure, exposure concentration, and failure dependence. Spreading fixed capital reduces risk toward a correlation-dependent floor, whereas repeatedly pledging the same collateral can make risk grow quadratically with breadth. We then study risk-sensitive allocators competing for fixed reward pools distributed proportionally to committed exposure. A single allocator has a unique optimum, and in a symmetric benchmark greater risk sensitivity encourages diversification under unique stake but discourages additional commitments under shared collateral. With multiple allocators, positive background stake guarantees a unique pure Nash equilibrium and supports a globally convergent projected method. Reproducible synthetic stress tests support these mechanisms. In the strongest common-factor environment, relaxing the reuse cap raises equilibrium reward by 2.47 times but aggregate 99% conditional value at risk by 3.77 times. Competition creates overexposure relative to a planner, while ignoring covariance raises true variance by 6.3%. The results provide a unified framework for collateral reuse, correlated operational risk, and incentive design in decentralized security markets.

papers.title: Counting solutions to Euclidean Fermat equations
papers.abstract: A solution $(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{Z}^3-\{(0,0,0)\}$ to a Fermat equation \begin{equation} \label{eq:abstract-gfe} Ax^a + By^b + Cz^c = 0 \end{equation} is called \emph{primitive} if $\gcd(x,y,z) = 1$. In the \emph{Euclidean} regime (that is, when the Euler characteristic $χ= \tfrac{1}{a} + \tfrac{1}{b} + \tfrac{1}{c} - 1$ is zero), the equation above defines a smooth genus one curve in a weighted projective plane. We study these models and provide an asymptotic formula for the number of primitive integral solutions with bounded height.

papers.title: Rømer all ears: An auditory analog of Ole Rømer's demonstration of the finite speed of light using smartphones as an acoustic vernier
papers.abstract: We present an undergraduate experiment for teaching Ole Rømer's 1676 method for demonstrating the finite speed of light. Two smartphones emit periodic sound pulses whose synchronization is evaluated directly by the participants' hearing, acting as an "acoustic vernier" that achieves millisecond travel-time resolution without microphones or external sensors. Because the measurement relies strictly on propagation delays between stationary stations, it establishes a direct experimental analogy to Rømer's original argument and dispenses with auxiliary wave phenomena absent from the 1676 analysis, such as acoustic beats or the Doppler effect. The pedagogical strength of the experiment lies precisely in this direct appeal to the senses. Loss of synchronization becomes perceptible starting at a separation of approximately 5 m and grows progressively clearer across several tens of meters. Despite its simplicity, systematic blind measurements determine the speed of sound in air with single-run uncertainties of 2 to 5 m/s (around 1%) and agree within 1.1% with theoretical predictions across ambient temperatures from 9 to 25 $^\circ$C. Beyond numerical measurement, anchoring the method in explicit sensory perception helps to clarify the recurring conceptual entanglement between Rømer's geometric delay and the kinematic Doppler effect, while highlighting how this same travel-time principle underpins contemporary astrophysical techniques, such as pulsar timing and eclipse timing variations (ETV).

papers.title: Classification of fast reaction limits for a two-component reaction-diffusion system
papers.abstract: We study fast reaction limits for a two-component reaction-diffusion system with four reaction exponents, in which only one component diffuses. For nonnegative segregated initial data, we classify the limits for all exponents at least one under homogeneous Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. The limiting equations include the heat equation, a one-phase Stefan problem, a fixed-domain heat equation, and a nonlinear equation with a time-integral reaction term. We also describe the limiting behavior of the nondiffusing component and obtain a nontrivial rescaled limit. In the critical regime, we characterize the limit as the greatest weak solution and establish a transition between initial finite propagation and instantaneous positivity. Under Dirichlet conditions, permanent zero regions may occur for certain small initial data.

papers.title: Differential Item Functioning: Methodological Advances in Detection, Identification, and Interpretation
papers.abstract: Differential item functioning (DIF) occurs when an item's response distribution differs across groups for respondents at the same level of the construct. Separating DIF from group differences in the construct itself requires identifying assumptions. Conventional analyses compare observed groups on a common scale established through items assumed to be invariant. We distinguish four settings according to whether the groups are observed or latent and whether the common scale is fixed by prespecified restrictions or estimated from the data. For observed groups, we review observed-score and item response theory procedures, multiple-covariate and intersectional models, and recursive partitioning. When anchors are unknown, we compare empirical anchor selection, partial and approximate invariance, robust scaling, regularisation and sparsity-based identification by the assumptions each makes about the pattern of DIF. For latent groups, we discuss mixture models and the joint estimation of class membership and DIF. Further topics include ordinal and multidimensional models, inference after data-dependent selection, effect sizes, consequences for composite scores, and the sources of DIF. We conclude with open problems, including anchor-free identification when DIF is widespread and inference when latent classes and invariant items are selected jointly.

papers.title: Dynamic Emulation for Bayesian Inverse Problems in Spatiotemporal Mechanistic Models
papers.abstract: Calibrating a spatiotemporal mechanistic model to field data is a Bayesian inverse problem in which every likelihood evaluation needs a simulator run. The R package *spDBL* replaces the simulator with a dynamic emulator, a matrix-variate dynamic linear model with a closed-form posterior that evolves the field in discrete time and processes large grids in spatial blocks. It then calibrates the parameters without further simulator runs, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (implemented in the Stan programming environment) conditionally on emulator draws. In benchmarks on epidemic fields, with every method tuned alike, *spDBL*'s predictions at untried inputs were the only ones with near-nominal interval coverage, though a tuned *RobustGaSP* was more accurate, and *spDBL*'s calibrations matched the accuracy of *RobustCalibration* with higher, though below nominal, interval coverage (80% against 67-76%) and over 50 times more effective samples per CPU second.

papers.title: CATWAY: Cost-sensitive agentic three-way robot decisions with calibrated language-model confidence
papers.abstract: A language-model robot agent must decide whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, and an unsafe execution costs far more than an unneeded question. No prior robot gate derives all its thresholds from error costs or acts on calibrated probabilities, and none was fitted in one domain and evaluated unchanged in another. We propose CATWAY, a cost-sensitive three-way decision gate: a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe) fixes execute, ask and refuse regions on the probability simplex, the question being the information-gathering step. Its probabilities fuse a ten-sample vote with graded scores of ambiguity, infeasibility and risk by logistic regression. Fitted on household instructions and frozen, CATWAY was tested on text-level decisions of three small models in-domain, in two new robot domains and on the external TRUST-NAV benchmark. At eleven generations per decision against one, it was significantly cheaper than a direct prompt, a cost-aware prompt and an unguarded agent in all 18 household comparisons (mean loss per item 0.28 against 0.57-0.83), in 9 of 18 in the new domains and in 10 of 18 on TRUST-NAV (Holm per set), and never significantly costlier. It executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions. On a unanimous vote, the minimum-expected-loss rule reduces calibration to one loss-derived threshold, so for two of six model configurations a gate on the vote alone never executed a clear instruction, costing 0.49 per item on TRUST-NAV against CATWAY's 0.13 and 0.09; the fused estimate avoided this on every set.

papers.title: Rapid Exploratory Maps and their potential role in supporting evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes
papers.abstract: Producing useful evidence syntheses requires clearly formulated research questions linked to an understanding of their optimal scope. When policymakers (or other end users) commission or steer the production of systematic reviews or other evidence syntheses to fulfil a demand for evidence, these parameters are rarely specified sufficiently for production to proceed. Instead, these details are typically developed via a collaborative dialogic process involving evidence producers and users to ensure the resulting synthesis will meet users' needs. This process is informed by scoping and (more-or-less formally) mapping the existing evidence base, which can take many weeks or months, slowed by applying mostly manual processes to identify and characterise the evidence. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have opened up new opportunities for more rapid, iterative, and responsive mapping of relevant evidence to support such early-stage evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes. In this article, we outline and characterise this emerging approach, termed Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs). We also present two illustrative case studies drawn from first-hand experiences within a programme of evidence reviews production to inform government policy in England. While this approach could be transformative for the mapping process, its broader potential is as yet largely unassessed, and it confers important challenges and likely risks, as well as benefits. Determining whether REMs could usefully support more efficient ways of working with end users when developing and designing evidence syntheses will require continued development and careful evaluation.

papers.title: Compositional Symbolic Execution à la Carte (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: We introduce compositional symbolic execution à la carte, a modular approach for building compositional symbolic execution (CSE) tools, powered by combinator-based design of key components, including memory models, management and automation of user-defined predicates, and bi-abductive analysis. Our approach is grounded on meta-theory mechanised in the Rocq proof assistant and allows tool developers to easily build correct-by-construction CSE tools for symbolic analysis of their programming languages of choice, with minimal implementation and proof effort. We show how our approach scales to real-world languages by implementing it in Gillian, a state-of-the-art CSE tool, and using it to capture the intricacies of the memory models of C, JavaScript, and Rust. We evaluate our approach by running all of the relevant previous case studies of Gillian, showing no unexpected behaviours and comparable performance.

papers.title: Heights and energies of polarized fibrations of varieties II. Fibrations over a polarized base
papers.abstract: We extend the height and energy inequalities for fibrations over curves to a fibration $f:X\to Y$ over a polarized variety $(Y,B)$. For an integrable relatively nef adelic line bundle $\bar L$, we prove a height inequality under the assumption that $L$ is nef on the inverse image of a geometric generic complete-intersection curve in $Y$. We deduce a lower bound for the local energy at almost every complex or nonarchimedean realization of a fixed polarized model when $L$ is $f$-ample. For a slope semistable bundle on a fixed polarized complex variety, we show that the infimum of the energy on its projective bundle equals the infimum of Donaldson's functional on Hermitian quotient metrics, with the normalization given below.

papers.title: GRUN: Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network for Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Image restoration remains a fundamental challenge in low-level vision, requiring methods that handle diverse degradations while preserving scene structures and details. We revisit classical Retinex theory and propose a Generalized Retinex formulation that extends the illumination-reflectance decomposition into a Retinex-inspired content-environment factorization prior for image restoration. The key idea is to restore images using two learned factors: a content-dominant response (generalized reflectance) capturing scene properties and an environment-side response (generalized illumination) encoding task-dependent variations associated with the observed degradations. Based on this formulation, we develop GRUN (Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network), a MAP-guided deep unfolding framework that alternates reflectance restoration, illumination estimation, and progressive degradation inference across K stages with degradation-conditioned proximal operators. We further introduce a Degradation-aware Coupling Regularizer (DCR) that combines mutual information minimization, gradient decorrelation, and scale anchoring to promote complementary content-environment factor representations. Experiments on seven image restoration tasks, including denoising, dehazing, deraining, low-light enhancement, deblurring, underwater enhancement, and backlit enhancement, demonstrate competitive results on multiple benchmarks using the same architecture with task-specific weights. Moreover, the proposed Generalized Retinex design can be integrated into existing restoration methods, demonstrating its cross-architecture applicability. Code will be released.

papers.title: GeoMVGen: Joint Appearance-Geometry Modeling for Multi-View Video Generation in Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires predicting how robot-object interactions evolve over time, encompassing both visual appearance and scene geometry. In multi-camera settings, such predictions need to capture the evolving 3D scene consistently across viewpoints, while supporting controllable generation under different robot actions and camera configurations. Existing video generation models provide strong priors for visual appearance and motion but typically lack explicit geometric modeling. Meanwhile, recent advances in geometry-aware and multi-view generation have explored joint appearance-geometry modeling and cross-view consistency, yet generating temporally coherent appearance and geometry across multiple viewpoints under robotic manipulation conditions remains challenging. In this work, we propose GeoMVGen, a framework for joint multi-view RGB and pointmap video generation in robotic manipulation. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework employs modality-specific adaptation modules to capture the distinct characteristics of appearance and geometry, while using cross-modal residual connections to facilitate information exchange between the two modalities. To establish geometric correspondences across viewpoints, we further introduce a cross-view projection mechanism with complementary geometric supervisions, combining pointmap consistency with geometry foundation model-guided feature alignment. These designs enable controllable generation of temporally evolving multi-view observations with coherent appearance and geometrically consistent scene structures. Extensive experiments on 4D video generation dataset comprising simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios demonstrate that GeoMVGen outperforms state-of-the-art methods in video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency.

papers.title: Harvesting Apple's Orchard: A Security Analysis of On-Device CoreML Models Across the Apple Ecosystem
papers.abstract: Apple ships hundreds of task-specific machine-learning models inside iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS. We present, to our knowledge, the first systematic security analysis of this on-device surface. We harvested 1,137 CoreML artifacts from six platform images and two device harvests, and a conversion pipeline recovered 155 previously opaque bundles as loadable mlpackage archives. Eight findings. (1) 368 of 1,137 artifacts expose plaintext learned parameters (281 blobs, 369.61 MiB) and 166 of 166 MIL bundles leak internal model-database tokens. (2) Specification versions 1-9 coexist and locale variants diverge architecturally. (3) Across 82,092 adversarial evaluations (221 model paths), worst-case flip rates reach 100%; zero-width spaces flip 65% of the Indian-English and 70% of the US-English SMS filter. (4) A 16-byte weight edit flips 7 of 8 probe inputs of a system model, with no runtime integrity check observed. (5) Loading Apple's own hand-gesture model crashes libBNNS through the public CoreML API (4/4 on production M2, also macOS 27.0); Apple ruled it a self-crash outside the security boundary. (6) Eleven bundles ship isUpdatable=1 hooks. (7) SMS text-classifier latency is 13.1-52.0 ms, 92.4% in the CPU-side NLP core, not the ANE. (8) The classifiers label 8-9 of 10 phishing messages Transactional. We filed three reports with Apple Product; all were declined as not crossing a security boundary, and we report the findings as robustness results.

papers.title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.

papers.title: Right Destination, Wrong Journey: Synthetic Counseling Dialogues Miss Human Interactional Dynamics
papers.abstract: LLM-generated counseling dialogues are increasingly used for training and evaluating mental-health systems, yet existing evaluations focus largely on response quality and final outcomes rather than how support unfolds over time. We conduct a trajectory-centered evaluation of process fidelity across ten human, reconstructed, and synthetic counseling datasets. Our results show that synthetic dialogues often reach plausible endpoints but differ from human support in recovery dynamics and turn-by-turn responsiveness. While generation design can shift global properties such as recovery timing and trajectory structure, contingent patient--counselor responsiveness remains consistently lower in fidelity across models and generation paradigms. Our experiments on controlled synthetic datasets show that targeted generation interventions can narrow the gap with real data on several trajectory-level measures, but do not fully recover interactional fidelity, with turn-level responsiveness remaining limited. We release three controlled synthetic datasets comprising 2,050 dialogues, together with annotations and the evaluation framework.

papers.title: A Constant-Factor Single-Sample Prophet Inequality for Subadditive Valuations
papers.abstract: We establish a constant-factor single-sample prophet inequality for online combinatorial allocation with monotone subadditive valuations. Given one independent sample from each buyer's unknown distribution, our reduction converts any offline algorithm achieving an $α$ fraction of optimal welfare into an online algorithm achieving an $α/120$ fraction of the expected offline optimum. The guarantee holds for arbitrary arrival orders and extends to the stronger Game of Googol model. Our approach has two key ingredients: a prior-free random score generator and a new sample-based construction of tentative allocations. The tentative allocations capture substantial welfare while controlling contention for items, and the score generator relates itemwise competition in the tentative allocations to the value of retained bundles. The reduction is efficient whenever its offline allocator and score generator are efficient.

papers.title: CROSS-Calib: Selective Channel Calibration for Ultrasound Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging provides views of internal tissue in real time for medical diagnosis. However, ultrasound signals may be affected by interference, and correcting errors and removing transient interference while preserving valid echoes remains challenging. We propose CROSS-Calib, a channel recovery method that uses predictions from other channels as references for amplitude and phase calibration, while a gate using context selectively combines calibrated measurements with predicted echoes to retain usable samples and repair unreliable ones. On the in vivo test set, CROSS-Calib outperforms all baseline models under gain errors and transient interference, while phantom tests show that the model restores cyst contrast with echo widths of wire targets close to the clean reference. CROSS-Calib can perform channel calibration and selective repair before beamforming to improve echo usability and image quality.

papers.title: The local intertwining relation for inner forms of $\mathrm{GL}_N$
papers.abstract: The local intertwining relation for inner forms of general linear groups over a local field asserts that the normalized intertwining operator for every parabolically induced representation arising from a local A-parameter is the identity operator. Our main theorem verifies the claim over local fields of characteristic zero. This will serve as a vital ingredient for completing the local intertwining relation and endoscopic classification for non-quasi-split unitary groups.

papers.title: LimoBench: How Street Smart Are Large Language Models?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.

papers.title: Your bids are showing: re-identifying power plants in anonymized market data, and a differentially private alternative
papers.abstract: ERCOT publishes every generator's hourly offer curve 60 days after the operating day. Market monitors, researchers and traders use these records to study the merit order and check for withholding. PJM publishes the same kind of data with unit names replaced by codes, on the view that masking keeps offers confidential. We test that view on ERCOT data from 2024 to 2026, where names are public and so provide ground truth, by masking the records under PJM's published rules. Public EIA and EPA data match 25% of the masked units we can score (32% of their capacity) to their plant, and 45% fall within the top five guesses. PJM's feed carries the same fields, so we expect masking to fail there too. Publishing exact fuel-group totals instead does not help. An attacker who knows the other units in a group recovers one unit's high-price offers exactly, and an outsider who knows only the target's outage dates reaches a correlation of 0.77, most of it from a few renewable and hydro units that offer at very high prices (0.32 over fossil units). We propose a differentially private release: monthly totals by fuel group and price bin, with Gaussian noise calibrated under zero-concentrated differential privacy so that each unit's whole year of offers is protected. It publishes an unbiased noisy layer and derives a monotone supply curve and shares from it at no extra privacy cost. At $\varepsilon=10$ per unit-year the market supply curve stays within 11% of the truth, the implied clearing price within \$3.0/MWh, and the attacker's correlation falls to 0.23. Whether an analysis still works depends on one ratio, how much the true quantity varies month to month against the noise, which predicts the accuracy of totals to within 0.05. The clearing price, supply slope and combined-cycle capacity remain usable, but no monthly release, private or exact, can answer questions about single hours or single units.

papers.title: Curvature-Equilibrated Policy Optimization for Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Gradient-based actor optimization is central to deep reinforcement learning. However, conventional first-order optimizers do not explicitly exploit the local curvature of neural actor losses. We propose EQUIP (Curvature-Equilibrated Gradients for Policy Search), a novel approach that seeks to balance local contraction and expansion of the actor parameter space by equilibrating positive and negative curvature. EQUIP constructs a trajectory-informed search subspace and uses the projected Hessian of actor loss to build a bounded local metric for curvature equilibration. First-order loss matching preserves the approximated first-order decrease in actor loss. Meanwhile, gradient mixing and curvature-based gradient selection adjust the gradient applied for actor optimization. We establish the geometric properties of curvature equilibration, derive bounds on gradient alignment and magnitude, and identify conditions for improved actor loss reduction and convergence toward stationarity under direct gradient updates. We integrate EQUIP into Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) without modifying its actor loss, critic learning, or replay mechanism. Experiments on 6 MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks show that the resulting EQUIP-SAC algorithm achieves higher mean sample efficiency than SAC and two second-order policy optimization baselines. Ablation studies further highlight the benefits of curvature equilibration and trajectory-informed geometry for policy training.

papers.title: Rethinking Document Indexing for LLM-based Analysis
papers.abstract: Documents such as clinical records, legal contracts, and scientific papers are increasingly analyzed with large language models (LLMs). The naïve approach of prompting the model with the full text for every question is slow, expensive, prone to hallucination on long inputs, and reuses no work across questions. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems build reusable state to address this, but they store it as embedded chunks: slicing text into fragments can lose the meaning that spans them, and the resulting index is tied to one embedding model, so it must be rebuilt whenever that model changes. Answering many questions over a large body of data without a full rescan, however, is not a new problem: it is the problem database indexes have been solving for decades, and we argue that this accumulated index design knowledge is waiting to be revisited for LLM access. As a concrete starting point, we propose Periplus, a hierarchical plain-text index inspired by the classic B+ tree. It arranges a document into pages running from general summaries at the root to specific ones at the leaves, so that each level guides the search into the next. But it departs from the B+ tree in three ways suited to LLM access: content lives at every level, the pages are plain text rather than attribute values, and navigation follows the relevance of a page summary to the question rather than a key comparison. The structure itself is discovered per document by the LLM rather than hand-designed in advance. In a preliminary evaluation on narrative and contract corpora, Periplus comes within 0.1--0.9 percentage points of the strongest baseline's accuracy while consuming 70--72\% fewer total tokens. These early results are encouraging, and they offer only a glimpse of what index design can bring to LLM-based analysis.

papers.title: $AdS$ Leading Regge Trajectory from String Field Theory
papers.abstract: We determine the $AdS$ mass of the leading Regge trajectory in superstring backgrounds $AdS_5\times S^5$, $AdS_4\times\mathbb{CP}^3$, and $AdS_3\times S^3\times{\cal M}_4$ with pure Ramond-Ramond (RR) flux for both ${\cal M}_4=S^3\times S^1$ and ${\cal M}_4=T^4$, to the second order in the expansion with respect to the background RR flux by solving the linearized equations of motion in closed superstring field theory. The $AdS_5$ and $AdS_4$ results are in a complete agreement with those obtained from the integrability approach to dual gauge theories, thereby providing a nontrivial check of the holographic duality beyond supersymmetry-protected quantities.

papers.title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.

papers.title: Exact Collision Gradients for Ellipsoids in Differentiable Simulation
papers.abstract: Differentiable simulation enables gradient-based optimization in learning and control problems involving collisions, but its gradients are least reliable at the moment of impact, when the velocities jump. A fixed-step simulator detects a collision only after the bodies overlap, and some differentiable simulators correct for this with a linear estimate of the time of impact. In this paper, we study impacts between ellipsoids. We show that the gradient error of this estimate grows with the obliqueness of the collision, the curvature at contact, and the time step, and that ignoring spin adds a further error. Subsequently, we find the time of impact with continuous collision detection on the Perram Wertheim contact function and differentiate through the touching condition rather than the search. This gives exact gradients at any step size. We demonstrate our method on an optimal control problem and a system identification problem. In both, exact gradients recover the optimal control and the true parameters, while the linear estimate does not, even when it accounts for spin.

papers.title: Generalized Tate--Nakayama duality for complexes of tori over local function fields
papers.abstract: We define the cohomology set $H^{1}(\mathcal{E}, Z \to T \to U)$ for a complex $Z \to T \to U$ with $T$, $U$ tori over a local function field $F$ and $Z$ a finite subgroup of $T$, where $\mathcal{E}$ is the gerbe from [Dil23]. We follow the method of [Kal26] and prove that the Tate--Nakayama isomorphism [Dil23, Theorem 4.10] for $H^{1}(\mathcal{E}, Z \to T)$ extends to $H^{1}(\mathcal{E}, Z \to T \to U)$, which lets one generalize Kaletha's parametrization [Kal21] of supercuspidal $L$-packets to local function fields.

papers.title: Translation Validation of SystemVerilog-to-SystemC RTL Conversion by Reading the Generated C++
papers.abstract: SystemC models of register-transfer level (RTL) designs are used for virtual platforms, firmware bring-up and simulation without a commercial license, and more of them now come from translators and language models. A wrong model usually compiles, and it usually agrees with the RTL. SystemVerilog evaluates an 8-bit sum in 8 bits while C++ evaluates it in 64, so a translation that forgets one truncation keeps a carry the RTL drops, and only inputs near the top of the range show it. I built svcc, an open-source SystemVerilog-to-SystemC converter, and my first check of its output read the generated C++ with SystemVerilog's rules. That check passed two wrong models. The check that replaced it gives the generated header the meaning C++17 and SystemC give it and turns undefined behavior into proof obligations. It prints what it read as SystemVerilog with every width change explicit, then proves that equivalent to a netlist of the source by induction over registers matched by name. On 50 author-written designs it proves 45 and reports 5 as outside its model. In a mutation experiment it accepted none of the 17 mutants that compiled SystemC showed to be wrong. Of 2,184 modules from 16 open-source code bases, 1,185 conversions match Verilator in random co-simulation and the check proves 600 of them. The same runs found defects in the front end, in svcc and in Verilator.

papers.title: Medical Image Segmentation Is Now Just Another Coding Task
papers.abstract: For decades, every new medical image segmentation task has needed an expert, a dedicated architecture, and a framework such as nnU-Net. This is no longer the case: medical image segmentation is now just another coding task. Given only a task description, labeled data, and a CPU (with no segmentation framework, no pretrained weights, and no human in the loop), four off-the-shelf coding agents built segmenters for 13 tasks across four imaging modalities within hours, an ability that has emerged rather than been built. On the nine 2D tasks, their best programs reach 99% of the Dice of a GPU-trained nnU-Net. Like any code, a segmenter improves by being revised and checked, so we ask how far the same agents can improve their own segmentations and what unlocks further gains. On unseen cases there is no reference, so the agents inspect renderings of their own predictions: this alone lifts the worst tenth of cases by 0.09 Dice and cuts boundary error (HD95) by almost a quarter. Far more is within reach. Told the true Dice of each attempt, the same agents improve in all 14 matched pairs, rescue 85% of failed masks instead of 30%, and surpass the GPU-trained nnU-Net on average, by producing better masks rather than by choosing among them. What unlocks these gains is a quality signal, which neither visual inspection, nor more rounds, nor a quality estimator trained by the agents themselves yet supplies: we call this the quality blind spot. The ability to build and to repair is already present; the next advance will come not from another segmentation model, but from reference-free quality estimation that coding agents can call.

papers.title: Photocatalytic Water Splitting in GeC/ReS$_2$ van der Waals Heterostructures
papers.abstract: Photocatalytic water splitting is considered as one of the most promising approaches for the green hydrogen production. But the rapid recombination of photogenerated electron-hole pairs severely inhibits its photocatalytic efficiency. Construction of van der Waals heterostructures is a good way to suppress this recombination. However, in staggered band heterostructures, the charge transfer could occur either through the type-II or the direct Z-scheme mechanism. Therefore it is very important to identify which mechanism is dominant. In the present work, we systematically study the GeC/ReS$_2$ heterostructure using first-principles density functional theory (DFT). The system exhibits good thermodynamic, dynamic and thermal stability and an indirect band gap of 1.38 eV which greatly enhances the visible-light absorption. We find that the direct Z-scheme mechanism is the dominant interfacial charge transfer by analysing band alignment and Gibbs free energy pathways. The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) can be driven spontaneously in the pH range $4 \le \text{pH} \le 14$ under light irradiation for both type-II and Z-scheme pathways but the energy barrier is much lower for the Z-scheme mechanism. Moreover, the type-II mechanism is not suitable for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but the Z-scheme mechanism can promote HER well in the entire pH range ($0 \le \text{pH} \le 14$). Remarkably, the strain-free (pristine) condition exhibits a solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency of 41.40\%, well above the 10\% threshold for commercial viability. The STH efficiency is further enhanced to 60.68\% under a tensile strain of +6\%. To summarise, the Z-scheme strain-tunable GeC/ReS$_2$ heterostructure is a promising and efficient photocatalyst for overall water splitting.

papers.title: AeroPoint: Agentic AI for Intent-Driven Point Cloud Inspection in UAV-Edge Systems
papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-based Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) inspection generates dense point clouds that strain onboard computing and wireless bandwidth. Intent-based inspection allows operators to request objects, attributes, and spatial relationships through natural language. Answering these requests requires trans- lating intent into spatial queries and retrieving relevant evidence under UAV processing and communication constraints. This article presents AeroPoint, an agentic AI system combining onboard point cloud processing and knowledge graph construction with Large Language Model (LLM)-based retrieval planning at a ground edge server. The LLM translates inspection questions into structured requests, which the UAV executes to return selected graph evidence for answer generation. We evaluate the prototype in a power line inspection case study using 150 TS40K UAV LiDAR scenes and profile processing costs on NVIDIA Jetson Nano hardware. Retrieval experiments use graphs constructed from dataset-provided ground-truth semantic labels. Experimental results show that transmitted payload decreases from 3700 KB for complete point clouds to 3.1 KB for retrieval responses, while evaluated LLM routers achieve the highest graph retrieval completeness for relational queries.

papers.title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training
papers.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time.
