Given tight resource constraints, we ask what the optimal number $\{N_k^*: 1\le k \le L\}$ of shots per bit is: $$\arg \max_{\{N_k\}} \mathbb{P}(\text{all } L \text{ bits correct}) \text{s.t.} \sum_{k=1}^L w_k N_k \le W$$ We construct upper and lower surrogate objectives via concentration and anti-concentration inequalities and prove an asymptotic optimality guarantee for whenever the budget satisfies $W = \sum_{k=1}^L \frac{w_k}{c_k}(\ln L + ω(1))$, where $c_k=-\ln\left(2\sqrt{\left(1-\frac{q_k}{2} \right) \frac{q_k}{2}}\right)$, which, for $q_k\ll 1$, is proportional to $\ln\frac{1}{q_k}$. Optimizing the tractable lower surrogate yields a true success probability within a $(1-o(1))$ factor of the exact optimum. We observe that when resources are abundant, $W \gg \ln(L)\sum_{k=1}^L \frac{w_k}{c_k}$, optimal allocations are proportional to $\ 1/c_k$. However, when resources are sufficient but not abundant, $(\ln(L)+ω(1))\sum_k \frac{w_k}{c_k}\le W \le O\left( \ln(L)\cdot \sum_k \frac{w_k}{c_k}\right)$, an additional $-\frac{1}{c_k}\ln\frac{w_k}{c_k}$ correction accounts for error propagation from less-significant to more-significant bits.

papers.title: Measurement-induced dynamics and emergent symmetries of particles moving in a one-dimensional lattice
papers.abstract: Continuous measurements simultaneously reveal and modify the dynamics of a quantum system. In this work we consider the tunneling motion of particles between the sites of a one-dimensional lattice. We investigate how weak continuous probing of the occupation of a single lattice site induces entanglement and selects definite values for system properties such as wave function parity and permutation symmetry. Our simulations show how continuous measurement can steer systems of two and three particles, with no prior permutation symmetry, into stable bosonic, fermionic and parastatistical symmetry sectors.

papers.title: NEXUS: Perceptive Whole-Body Control for Terrain-Adaptive Teleoperation
papers.abstract: Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid robot to reproduce a human operator's behavior even when their terrains differ. This demands that the robot perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts accordingly, rather than copy the operator's motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains remain scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control. To enable whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains, we introduce NEXUS, a perceptive whole-body control framework that combines human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback. We first develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that efficiently generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus totaling nearly 1,000 hours, we train a perceptive whole-body controller through teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains. Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on the evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains, further validating the generalization of our method. Project website: https://nexus-humanoid.github.io/

papers.title: Surveying for Close Binaries among Lithium-rich Giants
papers.abstract: One of the scenarios proposed to explain low-mass red giants with anomalously high lithium (Li) abundances involves tidal interaction with a close binary companion. If dominant, this enrichment channel predicts an enhanced binary fraction among Li-rich giants relative to Li-normal ones. We aim to test the binary interaction scenario by using multi-epoch radial velocities (RVs) to measure the close binary fraction of a statistically robust sample of Li-rich giants. The surveyed sample contains both red clump (RC) and first-ascent red giant branch (RGB) targets, allowing us to examine potential differences in the binary fraction with evolutionary stage. We monitored 70 giants (40 RC and 30 RGB) using ESPRESSO at the VLT, 57 (32 RC and 25 RGB) of which already had four or more visits over a $\sim$7-month baseline; the analysis here is based on these latter targets. For the targets with RV variation larger than that expected for intrinsic jitter, we performed Monte Carlo simulations to estimate the probability that the observed RV variation is due to a stellar ($P_{SB}$) or substellar ($P_{SS}$) companion. After removing targets consistent with stellar jitter, 11 ($34 \pm 8$%) RC and eight ($32 \pm 9$%) RGB stars remained as binary candidates or stars with a companion. Of these 19, three targets ($16 \pm 8$% of the filtered sample) are confirmed stellar binaries. The distributions of $P_{SB}$ and $P_{SS}$ are statistically indistinguishable between the RC and RGB samples. We find no evidence in our current data for a binary fraction for Li-rich giants (in either evolutionary stage) larger than that expected for a regular Li-normal population, suggesting that binary interaction is unlikely to be the dominant mechanism driving Li enrichment. Extending the RV baseline to probe longer orbital periods will be important to continue exploring the plausibility of this scenario.

papers.title: ToolFence: Fine-Grained Authorization for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents can be redirected by attacker-controlled content into unauthorized actions. Existing tool-level guards may miss within-tool hijacking, where an attacker preserves the intended tool but changes a sensitive argument such as a recipient or destination. We present ToolFence, a provenance-aware dynamic authorization framework that combines model-based and rule-based judges to improve detection accuracy and efficiency. An LLM compiles the authenticated user request into typed, task-scoped capabilities specifying permitted tools, effects, argument sources, workflow stages, and budgets. A deterministic monitor based on Guarded Colored Petri Net (GCPN) checks each proposed call and its concrete argument values before execution. When a legitimate step requires a missing capability, an isolated LLM judge can review the action proposal and update the GCPN monitor. We evaluate ToolFence on AgentDojo, MCPTox, ASB, and AgentLAB on four different LLMs, covering environmental prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory poisoning, and long-horizon attacks. It achieves the lowest or tied-lowest attack success rate in 15 combinations. On AgentDojo with Qwen3-max, attack success falls from 21.2\% to 0\%, with a 2.0-percentage-point reduction in clean-task utility. A measured runtime subset incurs 1.63X overhead, versus 12.95X for CaMeL. Our code is released at https://github.com/PolyLiYJ/ToolFence_v2

papers.title: SimpleEvol: An Agent-Loop Framework for LLM-Driven Automated Heuristic Design with Minimal Human Priors
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for automated heuristic design (AHD), enabling iterative generation and refinement of heuristics. However, the dominant paradigm embeds LLMs as narrow, fixed components, such as crossover or mutation, within heavily hand-engineered evolutionary frameworks. We argue this misapprehends LLMs. It treats them as specialized tools rather than general reasoners, constrains them to low-level operations, and underutilizes their autonomy. Moreover, the extensive human priors in these frameworks violate the bitter lesson principle that general methods scaling with computation surpass hand-crafted solutions. This raises a key question: which AHD framework designs best convert stronger LLM capabilities into better heuristics? To address this, we propose metrics for LLM-driven AHD framework handcraftedness (AHI) and intelligence conversion efficiency (ICE). Evaluating ten LLMs across three challenging combinatorial optimization problems, we obtain a notable finding that frameworks with fewer human priors consistently yield higher ICE. Based on this finding, we propose SimpleEvol, an agent-loop framework for AHD which removes nearly all human priors and allows the LLM to operate autonomously. SimpleEvol consistently achieves the highest ICE, often by a large margin. Our results challenge the trend toward complex AHD pipelines and point to a lighter and more model-centric alternative, suggesting that reducing human priors is a more effective strategy to scale up with model intelligence. The source code is available at https://github.com/HenryZhu1029/SimpleEvol-Master.

papers.title: SkillCome: Group Contrast Skill Optimization with Dual Memory
papers.abstract: Skill evolution improves the capabilities of large language models by analyzing trajectories generated under a given skill and modifying the skill accordingly. Existing approaches typically generate a single trajectory per question. However, this provides insufficient optimization signals since it requires inferring effective skill edits from a solitary path. It is difficult to pinpoint which actions caused the failure in a failed trajectory, or to determine which actions in a successful one should be incorporated into the skill. Furthermore, they rely on a local batch of trajectories for analysis, making the optimization direction susceptible to noisy evidence. To address these, we propose SkillCome, a Skill-evolution method based on group Contrast optimization with dual memory. For each question, SkillCome generates trajectories and performs group contrast analysis to precisely identify key behavioral divergences between successful and failed trajectories, offering reliable optimization signals. The dual memory system further accumulates evidence from historical steps to track patterns shared across different groups, leading to more generalized optimization directions. Together, SkillCome builds a systematic optimization process that transforms experience from observed successful trajectories into reusable skills. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks spanning question answering, reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. SkillCome consistently outperforms baselines across five models of varying families and scales, with gains up to +5.69 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/tdlhl/SkillCome.

papers.title: Purlin: Separating Orchestration from the Datapath of Collectives
papers.abstract: Distributed inference depends on GPU collective communication that must keep pace with evolving hardware and specialized workloads. However, existing works often couple the semantics, orchestration (where and when data moves), and datapath (how data moves) of collective communication. This coupling makes it costly to adopt new hardware mechanisms and customize communication for applications. We present Purlin, a scale-up communication framework that separates these concerns. At the top of Purlin, we specify collectives as a transformation from an input to an output layout. In the middle, we introduce a shared protocol, Stage, Notify, And Consume (SNAC), which derives orchestration from these specifications. Below SNAC sits a hardware-specific datapath we call Atom, which implements two key data movement primitives for collectives: copy and reduce. This separation lets us customize collectives and adopt new hardware mechanisms while reusing orchestration via SNAC. We evaluate Purlin on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs. Across seven collectives, Purlin achieves latency speedups of up to 5.14x and bandwidth improvements of up to 4.50x over baselines. Integrated into SGLang, Purlin improves offline LLM serving throughput and interactivity by 1.13x on average and up to 1.37x over baselines. For online LLM inference, Purlin improves interactivity by 1.26x on average and up to 2.85x, with the largest gain occurring under overload. For diffusion image generation, Purlin reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.13x.

papers.title: Can Language Models Learn to Forecast Stock Prices
papers.abstract: Post-training has been shown to significantly improve language models' performance on tasks with verifiable outcomes, including mathematical reasoning, software engineering, and computer use. However, whether the same approach can improve forecasting in financial markets is much less clear. Compared with tasks with verifiable outcomes, not only are realized returns noisy, but even what constitutes a relevant information set for making effective predictions is not obvious a priori: the model must decide which observations to gather and then commit to a numerical judgment before the outcome is known. We study this question in a chronological stock-price sandbox, where a language model gathers price, volume, relative-performance, and market-context evidence and predicts a future return. We post-train Qwen3-4B with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on tool-use demonstrations, then proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a terminal reward given by the forecast score against the realized return. The resulting AURA-4B more than doubles the starting direction--magnitude score, from 20.94 to 43.31, and is comparable to frontier language models on this benchmark. Conditional magnitude agreement rises from 33.3 to 66.2, while directional accuracy changes from 62.9 to 65.4. SFT expands tool use, and PPO further increases the share of ranking and market-context queries. These results show that post-training can substantially improve financial forecasting performance, together with changes in how the model investigates the market, on this outcome-selected benchmark.

papers.title: Disentangling Lung-Cancer CT/LDCT AI: A Systematic Evidence Map of Clinical Tasks, Evidence Chains, and Translational Gaps
papers.abstract: \textbf{Background:} Artificial-intelligence studies using computed tomography (CT) for lung cancer are often broadly labelled ``prediction'' despite addressing clinically distinct tasks. \textbf{Methods:} We systematically mapped CT/low-dose CT (LDCT)-centered lung-cancer AI using five-database retrieval, full-text eligibility assessment, role-aware modality/omics extraction, clinical-task classification, and a Multi-Tier Evidence Graph (MTEG). \textbf{Results:} The final corpus comprised 278 studies (2016--2026): 216 Detection, 7 future Risk-prediction, and 55 Other studies. Clinical variables (96.0\%), 3-D CT/LDCT (74.5\%), and radiomics (64.0\%) predominated, whereas external validation (28.4\%), calibration (20.1\%), decision-curve analysis (13.3\%), longitudinal CT (17.3\%), and saliency/attribution XAI (21.6\%) were less frequent. The fixed-extraction MTEG comprised 359 nodes and 3,284 edges. Of 278 studies, 31 (11.15\%) covered all six substantive tiers, with the greatest attrition at reasoning/explanation. With explanation optional, 110 studies (39.6\%) covered the remaining five tiers. \textbf{Conclusions:} Overall, the literature is detection-dominated, genuine future risk prediction remains uncommon, and complete translational evidence chains are rare in the extracted map. Limited omics-role recall constrains interpretation of the mapped molecular-input frequencies.

papers.title: t-J model at 50
papers.abstract: I briefly overview the original formulation of the t-J model starting from Hubbard model, as well as stress its unique features, i.e., advantages and shortcomings when discussing its physical properties. Particular emphasis is put on a brief characterization of connection between magnetism, unconventional superconductivity, and the Mott-Hubbard localization of the correlated carriers in a narrow band. In the second part I summarize the model generalization to the three--orbital situation. The main purpose is to list some basic features of the physics associated with t--J model.

papers.title: The overlooked price feedback: Why simulations overstate distribution grid peaks from home batteries under real-time pricing
papers.abstract: Simulation studies of home batteries under real-time pricing commonly find that synchronized charging creates new peaks in distribution grids. Yet all home-battery simulation studies reviewed here treat wholesale prices as exogenous, ignoring the effect of battery dispatch on prices. Charging in low-price hours raises the wholesale price, which dampens the incentive to charge. In equilibrium, charging is spread out across hours. This paper examines how accounting for this feedback changes peaks in local grids. A simulation of household battery dispatch under real-time pricing, calibrated to German data, finds that, if half of households own a battery, exogenous prices raise the coincident import peak by 83 % relative to the no-battery benchmark. With endogenous prices, the same fleet reduces the peak by 6 %. This finding is robust across alternative price functions, price paths, peak measures, and scenario assumptions. While new local peaks remain possible where batteries are geographically concentrated, these results suggest that published studies overstate the local peak-load effects of price-responsive batteries.

papers.title: Relic Neutrinos Probing Small Scale Primordial Non-Gaussianity
papers.abstract: Relic neutrinos retain a record of electromagnetic entropy production after neutrino decoupling, probing primordial modes erased from the primary CMB. We derive the cubic photon number source from acoustic damping and its leading folded sensitive bispectrum window, with neutrino decoupling, thermalization, and acoustic coherence combined in a single response kernel. For excited initial states, this kernel filters the physical folded profile and yields a sharpness dependent transmission condition, directly connecting small scale primordial non-Gaussianity to relic neutrino capture rates.

papers.title: Loop Dropout: Regularizing Shared Updates in Looped Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped language models separate computational depth from parameter count by repeatedly applying the same transformer block. Adapting these models requires a shared update that remains effective as hidden states evolve throughout the recurrent computation. Our empirical analysis reveals a pronounced late-loop bias in standard low-rank adaptation (LoRA): the shared update provides limited adaptation at early loop positions. This imbalance motivates training shared updates under varying combinations of their applications. Randomly omitting adapter applications alone, however, does not improve task performance; it reduces expected update strength during training while leaving inference unchanged. We introduce Loop Dropout, which couples stochastic masking of adapter applications with inverse-survival rescaling to preserve expected update strength and promote effective adaptation across loops. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved mathematical reasoning across model sizes, adapter ranks and training recipes, with benefits extending to general instruction tuning and code generation. Loop Dropout outperforms existing LoRA variants and adapter regularizers, while further analysis shows stronger early-loop adaptation. Every backbone loop remains active, and inference applies the adapter at all loops using standard LoRA without additional trainable parameters or inference computation. Code is available at https://github.com/NUS-HPC-AI-Lab/loop-dropout.

papers.title: TraceDance: An Automated System for Building Agent Behavior Benchmarks from Real-World Agent Deployment Traces
papers.abstract: An agent can complete a task while exhibiting undesirable behavior during execution. Developers need tests for the specific behaviors encountered in deployment, beyond fixed benchmark suites. We present TraceDance, an agent system that constructs targeted benchmarks from deployment traces for user-specified undesirable behaviors. For efficient construction, Anchor-and-Confirm combines programmable retrieval with candidate-level confirmation by a Flash large language model (LLM), while the Anchor Synthesis Loop generates and revises specifications for custom behaviors. The benchmarks use decision-point continuation to evaluate an LLM's next turn at a recorded decision point with a behavior-specific rubric, without a reference answer or environment replay. Experiments in coding and general tool use draw on 252,557 sessions and produce 107 benchmarks with 4,125 instances, fulfilling 95.3% of build-target requests. Both human annotators confirm the requested behavior in 84% of sampled instances, and the automated grader's agreement with human pass/fail judgments is comparable to that between the annotators. Nine frontier LLMs achieve a mean pass rate of only 26.7%, showing that they still struggle to respond appropriately at the evaluated decision points. Analysis across behavior-specific benchmarks further reveals weaknesses in how current LLMs behave as agents. By turning deployment problems into targeted benchmarks, TraceDance could serve as a key component of the recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop.

papers.title: Constant-Memory Differentiable Light Tracing
papers.abstract: Reverse-mode differentiation of Monte Carlo light transport naively stores a computation graph that grows with path length, ruling it out for deep or high-sample simulation. Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) removes that cost for viewpoint path tracing by reconstructing paths from their seeds and replaying them backward in constant memory. The construction rests on a one-path-one-pixel property that light tracing lacks: one light path contributes to many pixels, and its per-vertex adjoints cannot be recovered during replay from constant-size state. We show this prevents a direct extension of PRB, and that buffering the per-vertex data stays linear in path length. We then evaluate two constant-memory formulations. Reservoir Light Replay Backpropagation compresses a path's sensor connections into one representative by weighted reservoir sampling, keeping two passes at the cost of a sampling decision. LRB-3-pass adds a traversal that accumulates downstream adjoints first, keeping every connection and matching naive automatic differentiation in expectation. Both support differentiating with fixed or parameter-dependent path sampling (detached and attached), and both extend to participating media. We validate against naive AD and finite differences, characterize the memory and runtime trade-offs, and recover specular and volumetric caustics by light tracing alone.

papers.title: Scaling Density Functional Theory with Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) strikes a practical balance between accuracy and computational cost in many problems of computational chemistry and materials science. However, many DFT calculations are limited by fixed atom-centered basis sets, which dictate how accuracy and cost scale with system size. We propose Gaussian Splatting for Density Functional Theory (GS-DFT), which represents molecular orbitals as a cloud of Gaussians whose positions, shapes, and mixing coefficients are optimized jointly by gradient descent to minimize the energy without training data. Conceptually, GS-DFT is 3D Gaussian splatting with the renderer replaced by quantum mechanics. We introduce two key solver components: adaptive density fitting with screening for efficient evaluation of two-electron integrals, and a regularized differentiable orthogonalization of the molecular orbitals. Empirically, the optimized basis reaches the accuracy of the largest conventional basis sets with a fraction of the parameters, converging systematically in energy, density, and nuclear forces. At equal parameter count, it captures the stretched-bond and anion physics that fixed bases only recover with specialized basis augmentation. The resulting solver exhibits quadratic peak memory scaling in the cloud size, allowing us to simulate systems of up to 2,742 atoms (10,406 electrons) without any modifications at triple-zeta scale using a single four-GPU node.

papers.title: Critical escape dynamics of an active particle moving on curved surfaces
papers.abstract: On the macroscopic scale, active (self-propelled) objects moving through complex environments are often subject to effects arising from both the curvature of the surrounding surface and external influences such as gravity. We study the Kramers escape problem for active Brownian particles in two settings: motion in an external potential driven solely by gradient forces, and motion on a curved manifold subject to an additional constant gravitational force. In the absence of translational noise, a sharp dynamical transition occurs when the self-propulsion velocity $v_0$ reaches a critical velocity $v_c$ required for an escape. Above this threshold, the escape rate $k$ follows a universal scaling form, $k \propto \exp\left[-\mathrm{const}(v_0-v_c)^{-γ}\right]$, with an exponent $γ=3/2$ for the escape in a potential and $γ=1/2$ for the escape on a curved manifold in the presence of gravity. These distinct exponents reveal how the interplay of activity, surface curvature, and gravity determines the critical escape dynamics. Our theoretical predictions are verified by numerical simulations.

papers.title: The maximum area of the convex hull of a polyhex
papers.abstract: A polyhex is a connected set of n cells of the regular hexagonal tiling, joined edge to edge, where each cell has area one. Kurz conjectured an upper bound for the area of the convex hull of a polyhex, after the corresponding problem for squares was solved. We prove that the convex hull of a polyhex with n cells has area at most one sixth of the ceiling of $n^2+14n/3$, and that for every n this value is attained by a path made of three straight runs of nearly equal length. This proves the conjecture of Kurz and improves his bound by 1/6 when n is divisible by 3. The proof bounds the hull of the cell centres and three of its widths with a spanning tree of the polyhex. The upper bound is formalised in the Lean 4 proof assistant with the Mathlib library. We also show that for every n the extremal polyhex is unique up to rotation, reflection and translation, which an exhaustive search had confirmed for at most 12 cells. The proof of uniqueness was generated by Claude at the request of Sascha Kurz, and it is also formalised in Lean.

papers.title: Stale Does Not Mean Unsafe: Measuring Commit-Guard Precision for Tool-Using LLM Agents in Simulated and Transactional Infrastructure
papers.abstract: Tool-using language models act on state that can change while they plan. A version check detects that change, but an audit update and a revoked approval have different consequences for a pending action. We study how commit guards distinguish changes that preserve an action's safety conditions from changes that invalidate them. ShiftGuard pairs both types of race across sixteen infrastructure operations and replays identical proposals under alternative guards. The primary simulator grid contains 3,456 frozen proposals from three models, with a separate 1,152-proposal replication on a fourth. We implement the same operations on PostgreSQL and score persisted effects with a requirements-based checker. Among benign races in the scripted PostgreSQL benchmark, the runtime-held version and global-epoch guards block 80% and 100%, respectively, while the row-local predicate guard blocks none. The predicate guard records zero unsafe writes on the declared benchmark conditions, and all five additional hazards outside its declared contract escape it. A version guard using the model's expected version permits unsafe writes on 4.9% of primary replay decisions. The runtime-held version guard records zero in the same replay. These results identify two design choices for agent tools: bind freshness tokens to runtime observations, and represent safety conditions explicitly at the point where the effect is applied.

papers.title: Magnetic Lifting of BIC Symmetry Protection Enables Nonreciprocal Beam Steering and Angular Information Encoding
papers.abstract: Symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum (SP-BICs) offer exceptional optical confinement but remain nonradiative. Here, we demonstrate that magnetically lifting their protecting symmetry enables nonreciprocal beam steering with intrinsic angular information encoding. In a magneto-optical photonic crystal slab, an in-plane magnetic field converts an SP-BIC into a radiative quasi-BIC and, together with vertical dielectric asymmetry, continuously displaces the associated band extremum away from the Gamma point. The steered beam exhibits two independent locking relations: its wavelength is locked to the elevation angle, while its polarization orientation is locked to the azimuthal angle. These relations embed complementary spectral and polarization information into the scanning beam, providing additional sensing channels for multidimensional LiDAR. Moreover, the nonreciprocal dispersion gives different resonance frequencies at opposite wave vectors, supporting resonant emission at +k while back-reflected light at the same frequency is off resonance at -k, opening a route to intrinsic self-isolation and reduced optical feedback. These findings establish a unified framework connecting magnetic beam steering, angular information encoding, and nonreciprocal feedback suppression, with prospects for compact reconfigurable light sources and integrated optical engines.

papers.title: Anchor and Perturb: Lazy Agent Remediation by Exploration Injection
papers.abstract: In MARL, teammates sharing a team reward propagated via $\partial Q_{\mathrm{tot}} / \partial Q_i$ can all receive credit for positive outcomes, even when some agents contribute near zero and never explore higher-return actions. Under standard uniform $ε$-greedy exploration, concurrent exploratory noise across all $N$ agents can obscure trivial contributions from individual agents, driving QMIX into late-stage policy regression. Current remedies heavily rely on auxiliary models, intrinsic reward shaping, or pre-trained offline value anchors. Therefore, we propose Anchor and Perturb (AnP), an online framework for remedying lazy agents without altering QMIX's network architecture, loss function, or task reward. Its automated variant, AnP-Auto, monitors a real-time Laziness Disparity Index $\mathcal{L}_i(t)$ built from relative Q-value spreads and empirical action entropy. Once training reaches a point where lazy agents may surface while team win rate remains below a mastery ceiling, exceeding the $\mathcal{L}_i(t)$ threshold triggers a bounded rank-1 ($M = 1$) exploration pulse with $ϕ$-annealed decay ($ϕ> 1$) on the lagging agent while holding all $N - 1$ teammates strictly greedy ($ε_{-i} = 0$). Following this, a $ϕ$-ramped cooldown gradually releases the teammates into uniform exploration without major disruption to the replay buffer. As a proof of concept, within a tightly budgeted regime covering up to 4,500 episodes, a heterogeneous 10-agent SMAC MMM benchmark across five paired random seeds revealed that AnP-Auto remedied vanilla QMIX's late-stage regression and improved terminal performance on all five seeds. The method raised the terminal 500-episode greedy win rate from 30.20% $\pm$ 4.28% to 37.20% $\pm$ 4.55% (+7.00 percentage points; paired $t = 3.65$, $p = 0.0217$) and evaluation return by +0.71 ($p = 0.0037$).

papers.title: Exact Ehrhart Series of Birkhoff Polytopes via Constant Terms and Finite-Field Evaluation
papers.abstract: The Ehrhart series of the $n$th Birkhoff polytope is $\sum_{r\geq0}H_n(r)z^r$, where $H_n(r)$ counts nonnegative integer $n\times n$ matrices whose row and column sums all equal $r$. We present an exact method for computing this series using constant terms and finite fields. A root filter expresses $H_n(r)$ as a weighted sum of the values $h_r(M)^n$, where $h_r$ is the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial and $M$ ranges over multisets of $m$th roots of unity with $m=r+1$. Constant-term cancellation reduces the evaluation of $h_r(M)$ to a sum over repeated elements $a$ of $M$. For a particular $a$ of multiplicity $μ_a$, the computation uses a generalized Todd coefficient of degree $μ_a-2$. Sums of $h_r(M)^n$ over selected multiplicity classes are handled using symmetric function techniques. Together with the remaining individual evaluations, this gives $O_n(m^{n-5}+m^4)$ field operations for each admissible prime and fixed $n\geq5$. An explicit bound and the Chinese remainder theorem recover the integer counts, and Ehrhart symmetry determines the full series. The same method applies to the World Cup problem, which counts the same matrices with diagonal entries required to be $0$. We prove correctness and compute complete Birkhoff series through order $14$ and World Cup series through order $13$. The Birkhoff series for orders $10$--$14$ and the World Cup series for orders $9$--$13$ are tabulated in the appendices.

papers.title: Evidence for the emergence of stellar magnetic fields during rapid mass transfer
papers.abstract: Binary interaction fundamentally alters the evolution of massive stars, yet the physical consequences of mass transfer remain poorly constrained. Here we present high-resolution spectroscopic observations of Plaskett's Star (HD 47129) that reveal small radial-velocity variations of its magnetic secondary, coherent with the system's 14.4 d orbital period. These measurements support an evolved, post-mass-transfer configuration in which the narrow-lined primary is a partially Roche-lobe-filling stripped star with a mass of $5.9^{+1.8}_{-1.4},M_\odot$, while the secondary is a $40.8^{+9.3}_{-6.7},M_\odot$, rapidly rotating magnetic accretor. The system provides a rare opportunity to observe the immediate aftermath of mass transfer in a massive binary and offers compelling new evidence linking binary interaction to the emergence of strong stellar magnetism. Because magnetic fields regulate angular-momentum loss and transport, their formation through mass transfer could alter the subsequent evolution of massive binaries, with consequences for stellar populations, supernova progenitors and yields, and the formation of gravitational-wave sources.

papers.title: When to Move: Online Repositioning of Movable Antenna Arrays Under a Long-Term Actuation Energy Budget
papers.abstract: Movable antenna (MA) arrays improve multiuser throughput by repositioning their elements, but mechanical movement reduces transmission time and consumes actuation energy. Changes in user configurations create nonuniform demand for repositioning over time, while each movement determines which positions are reachable in subsequent slots. Thus, online control must decide when to spend a limited actuation-energy budget, not only where to position the antennas. We formulate causal effective-throughput maximization under displacement-dependent movement delay, inter-slot reachability, and a long-term average actuation-energy constraint. We propose Lyapunov-based online movable-antenna repositioning (LOMA), which adjusts the price of movement through a virtual queue and solves the resulting nonconvex position problem via proximal minorization--maximization, accounting for nonsmooth movement delay and promoting sparse antenna updates. We establish monotone ascent of the smoothed per-slot objective, a finite-horizon sample-path energy bound, almost-sure long-term budget feasibility under a Gaussian fading model with bounded large-scale gains, and a state-matched throughput comparison separating temporal energy allocation from per-slot optimization error. Simulations show that LOMA concentrates actuation after intermittent user changes and improves effective throughput over optimized fixed arrays and a per-slot-budget counterpart, while continuous channel drift favors more frequent incremental repositioning. Additional simulations with pilot-based channel estimates in sparse millimeter-wave channels show that LOMA retains most of the throughput benefits of online repositioning while operating near its prescribed long-term actuation-energy budget.

papers.title: An irreducible decomposition of the Weil representation restricted to open compact subgroups
papers.abstract: For a $p$-adic field of any residual characteristic, we determine irreducible decompositions of the Weil representation restricted to the maximal open compact subgroups and the Iwahori subgroup by using the Schrödinger model. In particular, these decompositions show that the restrictions are multiplicity free.

papers.title: Stochastic optimisation method for estimating large deviations
papers.abstract: A stochastic optimisation method was recently proposed to efficiently compute large deviation functions, used in statistical physics to characterise the fluctuations of nonequilibrium systems, modelled as Markov processes. The method, called LDSTOP, combines numerical techniques from control theory and machine learning to iteratively construct the "driven process", a controlled version of the Markov process used as a model of nonequilibrium system that realises a given fluctuation or large deviation of that system in an optimal way. Compared to other methods based on spectral approximations, importance sampling, cloning or splitting, LDSTOP is simple, flexible, and scalable, as it works by simulating single trajectories that are gradually guided towards the driven process. Here, we illustrate these advantages by applying the method on the full range of Markov processes considered in applications, namely, discrete-time Markov chains, continuous-time jump processes, and diffusion processes. For each type, we define the objective function to be optimised, explain different options available for representing the driven process (using, e.g., neural networks), and provide implementation details through simple applications. With these contributions, we aim to showcase the method's efficiency, as well as its ease of use when combined with available machine learning packages, such as PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX, for simulating stochastic processes and solving high-dimensional optimisation problems.

papers.title: Constant-Coin Complete-Information Debates for $\mathsf{P}$ with Arbitrarily Small Strong Error
papers.abstract: We study complete-information debate systems in which a probabilistic finite-state verifier reads the alternating messages of a prover and a refuter. Demirci, Say, and Yakaryılmaz showed that every language in $\mathsf{P}$ has such debates checkable with a constant number of random bits and arbitrarily small weak error. Their strong-error construction, which also counts nontermination as failure, did not permit arbitrary error reduction. We close this gap: for every $L\in\mathsf{P}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a constant-space verifier using a constant number of private coin tosses that has perfect completeness and strong error at most $\varepsilon$. The verifier simulates a polynomial-time alternating multihead finite automaton, privately spot-checking one of its input heads. The key observation is that, on a nonmember, the refuter may concede any round in which the prover first misreports a head reading. This ensures termination against every prover when the refuter follows the specified strategy, and permits strong-error reduction by repetition.

papers.title: Bulk-edge sticking beyond the Perron mode in Gaussian softmax attention
papers.abstract: We study row-softmax self-attention with independent Gaussian query and key weights in the proportional regime, at fixed inverse temperature. Hayase, Collins, and Karakida proved Gaussian equivalence for the empirical squared singular-value distribution after removal of the Perron direction. A global law alone does not exclude finitely many nonleading outliers. We prove that no such outliers persist: the rescaled squared singular value $\ell s_k(A)^2$ converges in probability to the upper edge of their bulk law for every fixed $k\ge 2$. In fact, this convergence is uniform over any deterministic sublinear number of leading non-Perron indices. The proof uses an exact decomposition of the softmax normalization, conditions on the key matrix, identifies the conditional covariance exactly with a diagonally conjugated inner-product kernel, linearizes that kernel in operator norm, and applies the outside-support local law of Fan, Ma, Paquette, and Wang. A separate stability argument identifies the finite conditional deformed Marchenko-Pastur edge with the limiting bulk edge. We also derive a scalar formula for that edge throughout the proportional regime and recover the explicit square-model formula of Hayase, Collins, and Karakida, including its physical branch.

papers.title: First measurement of the forward rapidity dependence of $W$ boson transverse helicity fractions
papers.abstract: The transverse helicity fractions of $W$ bosons are measured as a function of the $W$ boson rapidity, $y_{W}$, in the range $0 \leq y_{W} \leq 5$ using $W\toμν_μ$ decays in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV recorded by the LHCb experiment and corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $5.1$ fb$^{-1}$. The fractions are extracted from a template fit to the muon transverse momentum and pseudorapidity. The results show a strong rapidity dependence and agree with next-to-leading-order Standard Model predictions, providing the first determination of the transverse helicity fractions of $W$ bosons in the forward region.
authors: U. De Freitas Carneiro Da Graca

papers.title: WM-VS: Progress-Aligned World Models for Closed-Loop Visual Servoing
papers.abstract: Closed-loop visual servoing requires predictions that indicate whether an action reduces task error, not only whether the action is plausible. We call this gap the prediction-control mismatch and introduce WM-VS, a target-centric progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing. Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy with action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization. On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches a corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent. These results link progress-aligned action consequences to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.

papers.title: Positive normalized solutions for a singular regularized $p(x)$-Laplacian Dirichlet problem
papers.abstract: We study a singular Dirichlet problem driven by a regularized $p(x)$-Laplacian under a prescribed modular constraint. We construct nonnegative constrained minimizers for nonsingular approximating problems and, under the stated variational and boundary-control hypotheses, obtain a positive normalized weak solution as the reaction regularization vanishes. The approximation preserves the prescribed modular and yields subsequential strong Sobolev convergence of the states together with convergence of their constraint multipliers, while the gradient regularization remains fixed. Finally, we present a normalized singular problem on the unit disk as an illustrative example.

papers.title: Affine dual Minkowski problem for general measures
papers.abstract: In 2025, the affine dual curvature measures $\widetilde{C}_m^a(K,\cdot)$ of convex body $K$ were introduced by Cai, Leng, Wu, and Xi, and the even Minkowski problem for the affine dual curvature measures was solved. In this paper, the necessary and sufficient condition of affine dual Minkowski problem for general measures with $m>1$ are proposed.

papers.title: Fractal Hyper-Trees I. Combinatorial foundations: definition, enumeration, invariants, morphisms and the algebra $\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb H\oplus M_3(\mathbb C)$
papers.abstract: Fractal Hyper-Trees (FHTs) are hypergraphs organized in levels: each level consists of disjoint connected clutters, and every edge strictly contains each lower component that it meets. Connected clutters and Schr{ö}der hierarchies are the two extreme cases. Every FHT decomposes uniquely into the children of its top component, which carry smaller FHTs, and a host, an arbitrary connected clutter on these children. This gives an exact recurrence by size and depth and a species equation; the counts begin 1, 1, 4, 23, 231, 16947, 490083358 and are exact through nine vertices. Four interior moves (fusion, fission, aggregation, explosion) connect the FHTs on a given vertex set; every FHT on at least two vertices descends to the star by moves at distance at most one from the root, and $κ-1$, with $κ$ the number of edges, is its distance to the star. For FHTs with automorphism group $S\_4$, twisting the real group algebra by the sign character gives $\mathbb{C}\oplus\mathbb{H}\oplus M\_3(\mathbb{C})$, the finite algebra of Connes' description of the Standard Model. Conversely this algebra determines the group up to isomorphism and the class of a real 2-cocycle. The axioms select neither the group nor the twist: with the twist fixed as the sign of the action on the vertices, the algebra occurs exactly when $\mathrm{Aut}\,F\cong S\_4$ and some automorphism is odd on the vertices, at every size $v\ge4$. Every finite group is the automorphism group of a flat FHT, and every faithful action on a finite connected simplicial complex is rigidified into a flat FHT with the same reduced integral homology. All computations are deposited and their kind (exhaustive, sampled, exact or numerical) is stated.

papers.title: PlainMap: a lightweight, restartable mapping pipeline for ancient and modern DNA
papers.abstract: Mapping sequencing reads to a reference genome requires preprocessing and alignment choices that can vary with library type, fragment length, sequencing platform, and reference genome. These considerations are particularly important for ancient and historical DNA, where short and damaged fragments complicate read mapping. We present PlainMap, a lightweight and restartable mapping pipeline for modern and degraded DNA sequencing data. PlainMap accepts a simple manifest of FASTQ files, identifies single-end and paired-end data from read headers, supports heterogeneous sequencing inputs, and provides alternative mapping strategies for modern and degraded DNA. Optional pilot subsampling allows users to rapidly compare mapped fragment recovery across different settings using identical subsets of raw data, without attempting to determine the most accurate mapping strategy. Chunking and checkpoint-based execution support processing large datasets and resuming interrupted analyses, allowing users to balance memory requirements, runtime, and restartability. PlainMap produces duplicate-filtered BAM files together with fragment-aware mapping and coverage statistics. Evaluation using heterogeneous Japanese sea lion and short-fragment cave hyena datasets demonstrated successful processing across mapping modes, consistent trimmed and merged read counts across chunk sizes, and recovery from interrupted analyses without repeating completed mapping steps. PlainMap is implemented as a single Bash script and is freely available at https://github.com/BiodiversityExtinction/PlainMap.

papers.title: Made in Hungary: Comments on the performance of generative language models
papers.abstract: In recent years, three initiatives have emerged to develop generative language models in Hungary. The motivation behind them is the same. For Hungarian, no model with the given capability existed, or existing English-centric models offered limited proficiency. A detailed examination of the corresponding studies, however, reveals several methodological limitations. First, the reliability of the evaluation protocols is questionable. Contrary to the findings of Csibi et al. [2026], evaluation under the recommended inference settings shows that Qwen3-4B achieves higher scores than Racka-4B, its Hungarian-adapted version. Data contamination is evident in the work of Yang et al. [2025d] and Szentmihályi et al. [2025], potentially biasing the reported results. Second, the training pipelines fall short of current best practices in corpus curation and data mixture, which risks wasting substantial compute on low-quality data. The lack of controlled ablations prevents reliable assessment of these choices. Third, none of the three papers assessed forgetting or capability loss. Testing the adapted models on a subset of the original benchmarks indicates performance decline in all three cases, especially Racka-4B. These observations emphasize the importance of rigorous experimental design in language model development, given the significant computational and financial costs involved.

papers.title: AI for Games in the Foundation Model Era
papers.abstract: Foundation models, alongside advances in learned game-world models, are reshaping AI across the game lifecycle. Beyond playing games, recent systems model players and game dynamics, support design and development, adapt player-facing experiences at runtime, and evaluate resulting artifacts. Yet these directions have evolved largely separately, obscuring which capabilities transfer across settings and which remain tied to particular games, engines, interfaces, or player populations. We organize the literature into six roles according to the immediate use of AI output: playing and acting; modeling players and games; designing games; building and maintaining games; generating and adapting at runtime; and testing and evaluating games. For each role, we examine what structure is supplied by the game or workflow, what AI learns or produces, which capabilities and artifacts transfer across settings and roles, and what evidence supports the claims. We identify cross-role connections: trajectories train world models, learned environments provide experience for agents, design specifications drive executable implementations, and play or testing feedback guides revision. Evaluation is most standardized for bounded game playing and selected learned environments, while persistent state in learned worlds, repeated software revision, validated player modeling, sustained runtime adaptation, and representative automated testing remain less established. The central challenge is to reuse or transfer outputs and capabilities across roles while re-establishing evidence for effectiveness in the game-specific contexts where they are used.

papers.title: Higher-Dimensional Slowly Rotating Black Holes in Nonlinear Electrodynamics
papers.abstract: We study slowly rotating, nonlinearly charged black holes in arbitrary spacetime dimension $d \geq 4$, using a generalized Lense--Thirring ansatz. Working to linear order in the rotation parameters, we solve the Einstein--nonlinear electrodynamics (NLE) field equations for restricted theories ${\cal L}({\cal S})$ depending on single invariant. We provide an extension of the four-dimensional "No Go theorem" proven in ArXiv:2203.01919 and demonstrate the uniqueness of Maxwell theory in $d \geq 4$. Similar to four dimensions, it is proven that the standard rotation generating trick fails to produce full rotating solutions for any nontrivial NLE in higher dimensions. We identify a family of NLE theories admitting slowly rotating solutions with vector potentials encoding rotation effect in Maxwell-like manner; in four dimensions this reproduces the previously found RegMax theory, while in $d\geq4$ we obtain the corresponding electric potential in closed form and the associated Lagrangian implicitly as a function of the radial coordinate.

papers.title: Integral cohomology of classical Artin groups: spherical types $A,C,D$ and affine types $\widetilde B,\widetilde C,\widetilde D$
papers.abstract: We determine the additive structure of the integral cohomology groups with trivial coefficients of the Artin groups in the spherical families $A_n,C_n,D_n$ and the affine families $\widetilde B_n,\widetilde C_n,\widetilde D_n$. We first compute the integral cohomology of braid groups by algebraic methods and then use the Salvetti complexes to express the cohomology of the remaining families in terms of these computations. The resulting descriptions apply in every admissible rank. For each family, we establish cohomological stabilization and show that the integral cohomology groups contain no elements of order $p^2$ for any prime $p$. We also give uniform generating series formulas describing the stable integral cohomology in terms of that of the braid groups.

papers.title: DynEoMT: Learning Object Dynamicity from Online Segmentation Queries
papers.abstract: Video segmentation models delineate and associate regions over time, but do not explicitly indicate whether they move independently of the camera. Query-based architectures propagate region representations across frames, raising a central question: can existing segmentation queries also support dynamicity prediction? We introduce DynEoMT, which adds a lightweight dynamicity head to existing segmentation queries without altering the segmentation or query-propagation architecture. To supervise this additional task, we generate class-agnostic pseudo-labels offline from camera-compensated optical flow. At inference, DynEoMT requires only the current frame and propagated queries, without explicit motion or geometric inputs. On VIPSeg, an MLP probe trained on frozen ViT-L queries achieves conditional balanced accuracy within 0.05 percentage points of full fine-tuning, suggesting that dynamicity-relevant information is already accessible in these representations. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, the ViT-B variant achieves conditional balanced accuracies of 84.30%, 67.98%, 68.59%, and 87.64%, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance with minimal overhead in the measured inference path.

papers.title: Local-to-Global Isometries in Standard-Norm Generalized Gyrovector Spaces
papers.abstract: Every bijective gyrometric isometry between nonempty connected open subsets of simply connected generalized gyrovector spaces (GGVs) with real value-line structure extends uniquely to a global bijective isometry. The extension is a left gyrotranslation composed with an isometry preserving the identity, gyroaddition, and scalar multiplication. Gyromidpoints and point reflections give continuation of local isometry germs. Without assuming simple connectedness, a global bijective isometric extension exists exactly when the germs of the map and its inverse are fixed by their respective monodromy actions. Continuity of each fixed-scalar multiplication map implies contractibility and hence simple connectedness. We construct standard-norm GGVs for $t>0$ on positive invertible cones of nonzero unital JB-algebras and, in dimension greater than one, on their projective cones. Power maps relate their gyrometrics to Thompson's and Hilbert's metrics, respectively, with equality at $t=1$. Thus for both metrics, bijective isometries between nonempty connected open subsets extend uniquely to global bijective isometries. We give proofs of the known Thompson and Hilbert isometry classifications, together with their power-coordinate forms for every $t>0$, using the GGV Mazur--Ulam theorem and recovering the Jordan structures from infinitesimal gyrations. Applications include a new proof of Mankiewicz's theorem on connected open subsets of real normed spaces and a local extension theorem for hyperbolic balls in real inner product spaces, including incomplete and infinite-dimensional spaces. We also give constructions for products and function spaces.

papers.title: Timelike Entanglement from Spacetime Density Matrices: A Lattice Realization
papers.abstract: We develop a systematic framework for timelike entanglement in a two-dimensional free real scalar field, connecting spacetime density matrices with Lorentzian twist-operator correlators through independent microscopic and continuum calculations. Extending Gaussian diagonalization to generally non-Hermitian reduced operators, we determine their complete nonzero spectra in the generic regular case, together with all integer Rényi moments. The real-time replica construction relates these moments to twist correlators, with quantitative agreement in both magnitude and phase for the full four-point function on a circle, the Dirichlet and Neumann boundary two-point functions, and the massive form-factor predictions. In the massless continuum theory with Dirichlet boundaries, we further establish a finite causally connected window in which all integer moments are real, while the even moments are strictly positive for arbitrary initial states. For Gaussian states, all integer moments are strictly positive, and the resulting Rényi entropies are real. These results demonstrate that causal connectedness alone is not sufficient for a nonzero imaginary part of timelike Rényi entropy.

papers.title: The density of long runs of non-$r$-free integers
papers.abstract: Fix $r\ge2$ and let $D_k$ be the natural density of the $n$ such that none of $n+1,\dots,n+k$ is $r$-free. We prove that $\log(1/D_k)=\frac{r-1}{ζ(r)}k\log k+\frac{r}{ζ(r)}k\log\log k-C_rk+o(k)$, where $C_r=\frac{1}{ζ(r)}((r-1)\logζ(r)+r-1+r\log\fracπ{r\sin(π/r)})$; for $r=2$ this is $C_2=\frac{6}{π^2}(1+\log\frac{π^4}{24})=1.4595513\dots$. This determines Mirsky's constant $α(h)$, the density of the $n$ with $s_{n+1}-s_n=h$ in the squarefree numbers, to the same precision. Previously the only known estimate was $\logα(h)\le-\frac54 h\log\log h+O(h)$; ours improves this by a factor of order $\log h/\log\log h$, and is two-sided. The upper bound rests on the observation that the primes $p\le z$ with $\prod_{p\le z}p^r\le\sqrt k$ sieve a window of length $k$ with no freedom of alignment, so that at least $(1/ζ(r)+o(1))k$ positions must be covered by $r$-th powers of distinct primes exceeding $k^{1/r}$. The resulting sum over injections is $m!e_m$ with $m\sim k/ζ(r)$, evaluated by a saddle point. For the lower bound the Chung-Erdos inequality recovers the full contribution of $m!e_m$ rather than merely its largest term, which is what makes the linear coefficient explicit. As a consequence the first-moment threshold for gaps between $r$-free numbers is $\frac{ζ(r)}{r-1}\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}(1-\frac{(1+o(1))\log\log\log x}{(r-1)\log\log x})$; for $r=2$ the constant is $π^2/6$, that of Erdos's 1951 lower bound. We also prove that every covering system of length $k$ has modulus at least $\exp((\frac{r}{ζ(r)}+o(1))k\log k)$, so the Chinese remainder construction yields only $ζ(r)/r$, half of $π^2/6$ when $r=2$. Erdos's bound is thus equivalent to the assertion that the first run of $k$ consecutive non-$r$-free integers occurs at the first-moment threshold, not at the scale set by the minimal modulus of a covering system.

papers.title: Positive Temperature Coefficient of Anisotropy due to $d^6L$ Groundstate in $ε$-Fe$_2$O$_3$
papers.abstract: Positive anisotropy temperature coefficients ($dK/dT>0$) usually arise from hybridization between magnetic 3d states and strongly spin-orbit-coupled (SOC) subsystems. Yet $ε$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ shows $dK/dT>0$ (125-200~K) without an obvious SOC partner. We study pure and Cr-doped $ε$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ across the transition from low temperature incommensurate to high-anisotropy magnetic phases. We identify a $d^6L$ groundstate in $ε$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ while reduced hybridization yields $d^6 + d^6L^2$ in the Cr-doped phase, highlighting metal-ligand hybridization as a route to tune magnetic, electronic and orbitronic properties.

papers.title: On the Recall Scaling Laws in Mamba: A Theoretical and Mechanistic Study via Hashing
papers.abstract: Associative Recall (AR) is the cognitive ability to learn and retrieve links between items in memory. In NLP, AR is used as a benchmark for evaluating the in-context memory capacity of architectures such as Mamba, and has been found to strongly correlate with language modeling performance. This paper explores AR from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability, aiming to reverse-engineer the exact internal algorithm used by Mamba to perform recall. Our key insight is that Mamba performs recall by implicitly learning linear hash functions, and we identify the low-level circuit that enables this behavior. Building on these findings and inspired by theoretical tools in similarity-preserving hashing, such as the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing AR, which we term Recall Scaling Laws. Given the vocabulary size and the number of facts in context, this framework allows us to (1) predict the embedding and state dimensions required for Mamba to achieve perfect recall, (2) predict recall success probability given the model dimensions, and (3) analyze multi-layer models and multi-head SSM patterns. Empirical results show that our theoretical findings are accurate and predictive, offering insights into how AR capacity scales with vocabulary, state, embedding size, and architecture.

papers.title: From Service Access to Capability Theft: Cloning Task-Solving Capabilities of Proprietary LLM Agents onto Weak Open-Weight Agents
papers.abstract: Proprietary LLM agents provide valuable specialized task-solving capabilities, yet limited service access may expose them to unauthorized capability theft. We investigate a previously underexplored strong-to-weak capability theft threat, where an adversary seeks to reconstruct a stronger proprietary agent's task-solving capabilities on a weaker, attacker-controlled agent. Our motivating study reveals a skill execution gap: even with access to the victim's authentic skills, a weaker agent fails to reproduce its task-solving performance, highlighting the execution asymmetry between stronger and weaker agents. Our key insight is that observable victim executions expose procedural knowledge that, when adapted to the execution capabilities of weaker agents, can enable capability reconstruction. We propose CapaTheft, which reconstructs capability-critical behaviors through workflow abstraction, differential gap diagnosis, and structured skill rewriting, without modifying the weaker agent's model, harness, or tools. Across 20 task scenarios comprising 600 instances and eight victim--attacker configurations, CapaTheft improves task pass rates by over 30% compared with direct skill reuse and recovers over 80% of the victim's capability advantage. Further evaluations demonstrate generalization to unseen instances, cross-system transferability, and the limited effectiveness of existing defenses. Our findings reveal that observable execution information, when adapted to the execution capabilities of weaker agents, can enable strong-to-weak task-solving capability theft without further victim access.

papers.title: Planetary gas gaps and kinematic signatures in the planet forming disk around WISPIT 2
papers.abstract: The giant planet formation process in disks of gas and dust surrounding young stars is observationally still poorly constrained. Direct detection of protoplanets within the disk remains limited with current facilities. Indirect observational evidence of protoplanets through substructures or deviations from Keplerian rotation in the gas remains ambiguous in absence of detected planets. The lack of the combined detection of substructures and their corresponding planets makes it challenging to connect the planet formation process to the host environment. Observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) reveal clear detections of gas gaps and kinematic signatures in the WISPIT 2 protoplanetary disk that are cospatial with the locations of previously detected giant protoplanets. The newly identified gas gaps, observed in both the 12CO integrated intensity map and its rotation curve, correspond with the previously identified gaps in scattered light. Their morphologies are shown to be consistent with eccentric gaps, as expected from planet-disk interaction models of massive planets. The lack of eccentricity in the outer disk can be explained if a third planet is present in the system. The observations of WISPIT 2 provide a long-sought empirical bridge between kinematic signatures, gas gaps and giant planet formation in disks.

papers.title: When Do Frozen VLMs Respond to Image-Free Object-Token Edits?
papers.abstract: Answering what-if queries about a scene with a vision-language model (VLM) usually involves stating the assumption in text or editing the scene with a generative model. We instead move the edit to the representation level, before the model input. The image is represented as a set of object tokens, and the model receives edited tokens without accompanying patch tokens from the original image. This design rests on an open question: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to image-free object-token edits? We study this question in a simple testbed, keeping the visual encoder and language backbone frozen and training only a projector. Our analysis reveals three findings. Responsiveness depends on training: unlike standard VQA training, explicit edit training produces responsiveness in dense scenes and strengthens it in sparse scenes, across deletion, movement, and addition. Token construction and context token count shape responsiveness: the observed differences between token constructions appear to reflect more than token count alone, and responsiveness tends to weaken as surrounding context grows. Standard VQA performance and edit responsiveness are distinct: the object-token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-form VQA accuracy, and responses depend on the input tokens. The observed trends in responsiveness, token construction, and VQA retain their direction across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen language backbones. We release the evaluation-question generator, measurement records, scoring logs, and code.

papers.title: Analysis of the two-body strong decays of the hidden-charm pentaquark states in QCD sum rules
papers.abstract: In the present work, we study the two-body strong decays of the hidden-charm pentaquark states with the quark content $uudc\bar c$ and the quantum numbers $I(J^P)=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}^-)$ in the framework of the three-point QCD sum rules. The initial pentaquark states are described by four local diquark-diquark-antiquark type interpolating currents with definite isospin. We construct the three-point correlation functions for the decay channels $P_c\to η_c p$, $J/ψp$, $Λ_c\bar D$, $Λ_c\bar D^{*}$ and $Σ_c\bar D$, and derive the corresponding QCD sum rules for the strong coupling constants. At the hadron side, the correlation functions are expressed in terms of the hadron masses, pole residues, decay constants and strong coupling constants. At the QCD side, they are calculated by carrying out the operator product expansion with the full quark propagators, where the vacuum condensates up to dimension 10 are taken into account. After matching the two representations and performing the double Borel transformations, we extract the strong coupling constants from the selected Lorentz structures. With the obtained coupling constants, we evaluate the partial decay widths and discuss the possible assignments of the corresponding pentaquark states. The numerical results indicate that two of the compact hidden-charm pentaquark states can be related to the $P_c(4312)$ and $P_c(4457)$, respectively, while the other two lower-mass states may be regarded as possible hidden-charm pentaquark candidates to be searched for in future experiments. The present results may be useful for identifying the hidden-charm pentaquark states in future experiments.

papers.title: ASCII Attack: Recontextualising Harmful Requests as Artistic Critique in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety alignment trains large language models (LLMs) to refuse harmful requests. However, a request can keep its operational content and still change how the model interprets it, and refusal training covers such "recontextualised" requests only weakly. To study this gap, we propose the ASCII Attack, a single-turn black-box jailbreak. It embeds a fully legible harmful request in an assembly of ASCII-art characters, presents it as artwork, and asks the model for "artistic feedback". ArtPrompt masks a sensitive word that the model must decode. In contrast, the ASCII Attack hides nothing and changes only the social frame of the request. In order to separate the effect of this frame from topic, model and decoding effects, we pair every framed prompt with a matched direct-question control on the same request. The control also omits the scene description and the missing-information list, so the contrast measures the framing bundle rather than the frame alone. Across eleven models and eight harm topics, the JailbreakBench classifier judges 62% of framed prompts harmful against 42% of their controls. With a single query, the ASCII Attack matches or exceeds ArtPrompt and DeepInception under four of five harm judges. We further show that the effect tracks the model more than the topic and does not fall with scale, which is consistent with mismatched generalisation.

papers.title: Sparse Readout Prism: Explaining Logit-Lens Scores in Features Instead of Tokens
papers.abstract: Lens methods interpret intermediate hidden states by transporting them to the final layer and decoding them through the unembedding matrix into token scores. Fitted lenses learn their transport map from a training corpus. We find that changing only the corpus can change token rankings for the same hidden state; we call this corpus conditionality. To test whether two differently fitted lenses share unembedding features, we introduce Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), which learns these features by reconstructing each unembedding row as a sparse combination of them. SRP measures each feature's contribution to a lens score without changing the lens's transport. Across six models, SRP reconstructs logit differences more accurately than geometric baselines. On Ministral-3-8B, English and Chinese Jacobian lenses disagree on the top token for all prompts at one layer in both comparisons, versus at most 10% for same-language refits at that layer. On Qwen3.5-9B, disagreement reaches 87% between English and German Jacobian lenses and 94% between English and Chinese ridge lenses. At one layer, SRP finds the same dominant feature in the two lenses' top-token scores for 81% of prompts with English and German Jacobian lenses on Qwen and up to 78% with English and Chinese Jacobian lenses on Ministral.

papers.title: On the interpretation of the kinetics of ligand-receptor binding
papers.abstract: When the rates of ligand binding are measured by methods such as surface plasmon resonance, it is common practice to use the observed rate constants for the onset and offset of binding to estimate an equilibrium constant for ligand binding. If this agrees with the equilibrium constant found as the EC50 for binding at equilibrium, this is taken as validation of the measured rates. This is correct only when binding produces no conformation change in the receptor, and ligand binding follows a single exponential time course. Here, we investigate a simple 3 state model in which binding is followed by a conformation change in the receptor. Three special cases of this model in which the time course of onset and offset of ligand binding are close to being single exponentials are analysed. These cases are (1) when binding is much faster than the conformation change, (2) when the conformation change is much faster than binding, and (3) when the rates of ligand dissociation and receptor activation are both fast. It is concluded that the measured rates will often yield an estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding that is close to the effective, or macroscopic, equilibrium constant, the EC50 found by measuring binding at equilibrium, which depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants describing ligand binding and the conformation change. The exception to this conclusion is the case when binding is much faster than the subsequent conformation change, though the estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding still depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants.

papers.title: Auslander correspondence for higher stable dg categories and cluster Morita theory
papers.abstract: We prove a cluster Morita theorem: every pretriangulated dg category with a $d$-cluster tilting subcategory is realized as the $d$-cluster dg category of that subcategory regarded as a connective dg category. Reversing the Amiot--Guo construction, this yields a bijection between $d$-stable dg categories and pretriangulated dg categories with a chosen $d$-cluster tilting subcategory. Our Auslander correspondence characterizes $d$-stability by coherence, weak global dimension at most $d+1$, and a $(d+1)$-shifted duality on finitely presented modules. For a locally finite $d$-stable dg algebra over a field, right $(d+1)$-Calabi--Yau structures on its perfectly valued derived dg category correspond bijectively to right $d$-Calabi--Yau structures on its $d$-cluster dg category. In characteristic zero, this removes the pseudo-compact enhancement hypothesis from Keller--Liu's theorem on Amiot's conjecture. Via Koszul duality, we characterize $d$-stability over any field for locally finite minimal completed dg path algebras (and their analogues for graded species) by explicit conditions on the graded arrows and the quadratic differential. For $d=1$, these are deformed derived mesh algebras of Dynkin type; for $d=2$, they are complete twisted Ginzburg dg algebras, yielding via cluster Morita theory a twisted analogue of Amiot's conjecture in arbitrary characteristic without a Calabi--Yau hypothesis.

papers.title: Update from Hell: Can Coding Agents Survive Hidden Breakage in Dependency Upgrades?
papers.abstract: Modern software systems rely heavily on third-party dependencies, but upgrading those dependencies remains a costly maintenance activity. Dependency upgrades do not always preserve the function signatures, type systems, APIs, or runtime semantics assumed by existing code. Consequently, developers often need to perform source code adaptations to accommodate dependency-induced changes. However, such code-level changes are often not explicitly communicated to project maintainers, posing a significant challenge to software reliability. Meanwhile, coding agents have emerged as a new form of software development tool and are increasingly adopted by developers due to their automation capabilities. In this paper, we introduce DEPBENCH, a benchmark consisting of 203 real-world dependency-upgrade tasks across five package ecosystems spanning five language communities, each involving hidden code-level changes that require source code adaptation. We evaluate mainstream coding agents on DEPBENCH. The best completed configuration solves only 104/203 tasks (51.2%), with substantial variation across agent harnesses, models, and ecosystems, highlighting an important gap between current agent capabilities and real-world software maintenance needs.

papers.title: Fermion mass hierarchies in a three-generation Clifford model
papers.abstract: We examine whether an algebraic model of three fermion generations based on the complex Clifford algebra $\mathbb C\ell(10)$, in which an $S_3$ family symmetry relates the generations, can reproduce the observed mass hierarchies of the charged leptons and down quarks. Taking the internal Gram matrix as the fermion kinetic metric, we show that the original Yukawa interaction, with complex coefficients, gives precisely those ordered mass triples $0\leq m_1\leq m_2\leq m_3$ for which $m_3\leq m_1+2m_2$. This restriction excludes the observed hierarchies in both sectors and persists when the right-acting Higgs operator is allowed to range over the full Clifford algebra. This obstruction motivates a second Yukawa contraction in which a projector, constructed from the difference between an internal charge operator and its family average, acts from the left. The resulting interaction preserves the gauge and family symmetries and uses the same three Higgs doublets. With both contractions present, there is a fixed coupling ratio at which the two successive mass ratios in a single sector become arbitrarily large along a real vacuum path. Separately, a rational interval calculation establishes that one real Higgs vacuum, with different coupling ratios in the two sectors, reproduces the chosen running masses of the charged leptons and down quarks. A softly broken three-doublet potential realises this vacuum as a global minimum at tree level. The additional neutral scalars have flavour-changing couplings, and their exchange at a common mass of $2000\,\mathrm{TeV}$ satisfies the neutral-meson mixing criterion and the $μ\to3e$ contact-interaction test considered here.

papers.title: WoE Wrote It? Watermarking Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Black-Box Text Provenance
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) watermarks provide a mechanism for text provenance, enabling model owners to identify machine-generated content and attribute it to a specific watermarked model. However, current LLM watermarking approaches predominantly rely on inference-time sampler methods and focus their analysis on dense models. Inference-time methods are only effective when the text is explicitly generated via the model owner's controlled API; they fail in a post-theft scenario. An adversary who steals or leaks the model weights gains complete control over inference and can simply run an unmodified sampler, bypassing the watermark and preventing post-theft attribution. In this work, we introduce Watermarking of Experts (WoE), a novel black-box text provenance method that leverages the unique structural properties of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. WoE biases the vocabulary of a few secret experts, and defenders detect it by replaying suspect text through their own checkpoint to recover where these experts acted. This approach ensures the watermark remains intrinsic to the model parameters, enabling defenders to attribute text generated by stolen weights, leaked checkpoints, and secondary dense models distilled from the stolen model without needing access to the adversary's deployment or weights. We evaluate WoE across eight MoE models, demonstrating successful watermark detection from suspect text, achieving an average true positive rate of 92.5% at a 1% false positive rate, reaching up to 95.3%, while reducing benchmark accuracy by only 0.4% on average.
